security.heroTitle: How we protect your account and your data
security.heroBody: Concrete measures we apply. No marketing, no vague promises: what the code actually does.

account.verifiedBody: Only trainers and caretakers who submitted an ID and were manually approved appear in search.
account.sessionsBody: If you lose your phone or suspect access, you can invalidate every active session with one tap.
account.reauthBody: Deleting your account or revoking sessions asks for your password again. An unlocked phone is not enough.
account.softDeleteBody: If you delete your account you can restore it for the next 30 days by signing back in. After that it's permanent.
account.emailAlertsBody: We email you when someone revokes all your sessions or requests account deletion, so you can react if it wasn't you.

chat.piiBody: If your message contains an email, phone number, or the name of another messaging app, we warn you before sending. Your call.
chat.onPlatformBody: Keeping chats here lets us review reports, retain evidence, and protect both sides in any dispute.
chat.reportBody: If someone offends you, harasses you, or tries to pull you off-platform, report it. We review manually.

location.foregroundBody: Live location is only active while the provider has the service open in the foreground. Never in the background.
location.anonymizedBody: When the walk ends we round the last GPS point to a ~500 m zone. The owner sees the route but not the carer's home.
location.photoBody: Photos the carer sends during the walk travel over HTTPS and are visible only to the two parties on the booking.

data.exportBody: From Settings → Download my data you get a JSON with your profile, dogs, bookings, reviews, transactions and more.
data.deleteBody: Deleting your account removes your profile, dogs, photos, reviews and associated messages from Firebase servers.
data.photoBody: You can sign up and book without a photo. We show your initials. If you uploaded one and changed your mind, you can remove it.
data.storageBody: Data stored on Google Cloud — Firestore in EU multi-region eur3 (Belgium + Netherlands) and Storage in europe-west1 (Belgium), encrypted at rest. Zero international transfers in normal operation.

security.contactSettingsBody: Revoke sessions, download data, delete account and more.
security.footer: This document is updated every time we add or change a security measure. Last review: May 11, 2026.

coursesPage.title: Training Courses
coursesPage.subtitle: From curious pup to exemplary companion

labels.positiveOnlyDesc: This course uses only positive reinforcement. No yelling, jerking or punishment.

sit.title: Sit
sit.subtitle: The first command every dog must learn
sit.objective: Teach the dog to sit when given the verbal command “sit”, holding the position until released by another signal.
why: Control the dog in everyday situations
Improve attention and focus
Serves as the foundation for any other training
benefits: Your dog will calm down at street crossings or when greeting visitors
Reduces the risk of jumping on children or elderly people
It's the foundation for advanced commands like “stay”, “down” or “shake”
Builds mutual trust from the very first day of living together
where: 🏠 At home (living room or quiet room)
🌿 In the garden or terrace
🔇 Without distractions at first
materials: 🫖 Small treats (soft food, pea-sized)
🦮 Short leash (optional, only if your dog gets distracted)
🛟 A mat or comfortable surface
💛 Patience and a calm voice
beforeYouStart: Your dog must be calm, not over-excited after an intense walk
Practice before meals (with mild appetite, never starving)
Choose a quiet place — no TV, other animals or visitors
Keep the treats ready in a waist pouch so you don't get distracted
Sessions of 5 minutes max: prefer quality over quantity

methods.title: Lure method (recommended)
methods.description: You guide the dog into position using a treat as a lure. The fastest and clearest method for beginners.
methods.bestFor: Puppies and dogs without prior training

steps.title: Get their attention
steps.description: Stand in front of your dog. Show the treat close to their nose to capture their attention.
steps.tip: Make sure they are looking at you before continuing.
steps.troubleshooting: If they don't look, raise the treat value (cheese, sausage).

steps.title: Guided movement
steps.description: Slowly move the treat upward and backward over their head. The dog will naturally lower their hips and sit.
steps.tip: Don't push them. Let the movement guide them.
steps.troubleshooting: If they back up instead of sitting, do it against a wall so they can't walk backward.

steps.title: Introduce the command
steps.description: Just as they sit, say clearly: “sit”. Always use the same word and same tone.
steps.tip: Timing is key: say the word at the exact moment they sit.

steps.title: Immediate reward
steps.description: Give the treat instantly and praise them with a happy, positive voice. The dog will associate “sit” with something good.
steps.tip: The reward must arrive within 2 seconds.

steps.title: Repeat and progress
steps.description: Do 5–10 repetitions per session, 2–3 sessions per day. Over time, reduce treats and reinforce with praise only.
steps.tip: Short sessions = better learning.

methods.title: Capture method (dogs that already sit on their own)
methods.description: You reward the dog every time they sit spontaneously, without asking. Works if your dog already tends to sit.
methods.bestFor: Adult dogs, rescues, or dogs afraid of hands near their face

steps.title: Observe and wait
steps.description: Walk calmly around the house with treats handy. Ignore the dog and go about your day.
steps.tip: It's important not to talk to or stare at the dog.

steps.title: Mark the moment
steps.description: As soon as the dog sits on their own initiative, say a clear “yes” or use the clicker at that exact instant.
steps.tip: The “yes” or click must arrive AT the exact moment the rear hits the floor.

steps.title: Reward instantly
steps.description: Toss a treat on the floor (not from the hand) so they get up again and can repeat the gesture.
steps.tip: Tossing the treat on the floor avoids dependence on your hand.

steps.title: Add the word
steps.description: Once they sit repeatedly to earn the treat, start saying “sit” just before they do it.
steps.tip: Only add the word once the behavior is predictable.

steps.title: Generalize
steps.description: Practice in different rooms, positions and times of day. Generalization is what makes the command always work.
steps.tip: Count how many times they get it right out of 10. Once you reach 8/10, change context.

commonErrors.error: Repeating the command many times in a row (“sit, sit, sit”)
commonErrors.cause: Frustration when they don't respond on the first try
commonErrors.fix: Say the command ONCE and wait 5 seconds in silence. If no response, go back to the lure step.

commonErrors.error: Rewarding late, when the dog has already stood up again
commonErrors.cause: Slow reflexes or treat out of reach
commonErrors.fix: Practice timing without the dog: toss a treat in the air and catch it within 2 seconds.

commonErrors.error: Pushing the back or hips to force the position
commonErrors.cause: Anxiety to see fast results
commonErrors.fix: Never touch physically. If they don't sit, improve the lure (treat closer to nose, slower motion).

commonErrors.error: Sessions too long that exhaust the dog
commonErrors.cause: More training ≠ better learning
commonErrors.fix: Maximum 5 minutes per session. Always end on a successful repetition, not a failure.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog looks at me but doesn't do anything
troubleshooting.solution: Bring the treat closer to their nose, almost touching it, and move it slower. If still no reaction, try a higher-value treat.

troubleshooting.problem: They jump to grab the treat instead of sitting
troubleshooting.solution: You're lowering your hand too much and then raising it too high. Keep the treat just above their head, not over.

troubleshooting.problem: Works at home but not on the street
troubleshooting.solution: It's normal. Repeat all steps from scratch in the new environment, with fewer distractions first (empty street, quiet park).

troubleshooting.problem: They sit but get up immediately
troubleshooting.solution: Reward faster (within 1 second) and, when correct, gradually increase seconds before rewarding (1s → 3s → 5s).

progressMilestones.goal: Your dog follows the treat with their nose and sits spontaneously at least once
Sits with the word “sit” 70% of the time at home in calm conditions
Sits without a visible treat, with voice command only
Holds the position 5–10 seconds before reward, at home and in the garden

successSigns: Sits when hearing the command without a visible treat
Does it in different locations (home, garden, quiet street)
Responds even with minor distractions
Holds the position until you give another signal
variations: Sit at 1 meter distance (without you in front)
Sit only with a hand gesture, no voice
Lateral sit (next to you, not facing you)
Sit while you sit down or stand up
Sit for 30 seconds before eating (self-control)
safetyNotes: Never force an older dog or one with arthritis to repeat the exercise if they show pain when sitting
If your dog pants heavily, walks away or avoids eye contact during several sessions, take a 24h break
Avoid very cold, hot or slippery surfaces (freshly waxed floors)
Puppies under 12 weeks: maximum 3 minutes per session
sit.funFact: Border Collies and Poodles learn “sit” in fewer than 5 repetitions. Bulldogs and Mastiffs may need 30 or more, but they retain it just as well.
sit.nextLevel: Practice “sit” outdoors with distractions (other dogs, noise). Then introduce “stay” for several minutes.
sit.proTip: Always train when the dog is slightly hungry (before meals). Treats work much better when the dog has an appetite. If your dog is very distracted, raise the treat value (from kibble to cheese or boiled chicken).

lie.title: Lie down
lie.subtitle: The next step after learning to sit
lie.objective: Teach the dog to lie down on the command “down”, holding the position for several seconds.
why: Calms the dog during exciting moments
Helps control situations in public spaces
Improves overall obedience
Natural progression after “sit”
benefits: Your dog will relax in restaurants, terraces or long visits
Ideal posture for prolonged rest and barking control
Foundation to teach “stay” for several minutes
Reduces reactivity: a dog lying down doesn't jump or lunge
where: 🏠 At home (comfortable floor, rug or living room)
🌿 Quiet garden
⛔ Avoid cold, hard or slippery surfaces at first
materials: 🫖 Small soft treats
🛏️ Mat or dog bed (recommended)
🦮 Short leash (optional)
💛 Patience and calm voice
beforeYouStart: Your dog must already know “sit” fluently
Make sure the surface is comfortable (no cold floor)
Train after a short walk: a slightly tired dog learns better
Have at least 15 small treats ready
Sessions of max 5 minutes

methods.title: L-shaped lure method (recommended)
methods.description: You guide the dog with a treat tracing an L: first downward between their paws, then forward.
methods.bestFor: Puppies and dogs that already know sit

steps.title: Starting position: sit
steps.description: Ask your dog to sit. This is the ideal starting point because the hips are already lowered.
steps.tip: If they don't respond fluently to sit, go back to that course first.
steps.troubleshooting: If they break the sit, calmly ask again without scolding.

steps.title: Downward motion
steps.description: Place the treat on their nose and slowly lower it to the floor between their front paws.
steps.tip: Slow, continuous motion, no pauses.
steps.troubleshooting: If they stand up, ask for sit again and restart slower.

steps.title: Forward motion
steps.description: Once the treat is on the floor, slide it forward in a straight line. The dog will stretch and lie down.
steps.tip: The full motion traces a capital L.

steps.title: Introduce the command
steps.description: Once fully lying (belly touching the floor), say clearly: “down”.
steps.tip: Only say the word when fully lying, not halfway.

steps.title: Reward and reinforce
steps.description: Give the treat immediately, on the floor between their paws. Praise with happy voice.
steps.tip: Rewarding on the floor reinforces the position and prevents standing.

steps.title: Increase duration
steps.description: When done on first try, wait 1 second before rewarding. Build to 3, 5, 10 seconds gradually.
steps.tip: If they break the position early, drop back to the previous duration.

methods.title: Raised platform method
methods.description: You use a low step or cushion: the dog is half-elevated, making it easier for front paws to slide forward.
methods.bestFor: Large dogs, anxious dogs, or those that don't respond to lure

steps.title: Place dog on a low cushion
steps.description: A 5–10 cm tall platform. Firm cushion, low step or yoga block.
steps.tip: The front edge must be free.

steps.title: Ask for sit on the platform
steps.description: The dog should sit on the cushion. Reward.
steps.tip: If uncomfortable on it, spend a few minutes familiarizing them.

steps.title: Lure forward
steps.description: Lure their front paws forward (off the platform). They'll naturally fall into the down position.
steps.tip: The trick: the elevated platform makes lying down physically easier.

steps.title: Mark and reward
steps.description: Once fully down, say “down” and reward.
steps.tip: Repeat until they associate the word.

steps.title: Remove the platform
steps.description: After 5–10 sessions with platform, try on flat ground. Should work the same.
steps.tip: If not, return to the platform 2–3 more sessions.

commonErrors.error: Pushing the dog down with your hand on the back
commonErrors.cause: Frustration when the lure doesn't work first try
commonErrors.fix: Never use physical force. Improve the lure motion or use the platform method.

commonErrors.error: Rewarding before fully down
commonErrors.cause: Anticipating success
commonErrors.fix: Wait until belly and elbows are on the floor before rewarding. Otherwise you reinforce intermediate positions.

commonErrors.error: Practicing on cold or slippery surfaces
commonErrors.cause: Lack of environmental planning
commonErrors.fix: Always use rug, bed or carpet. Dogs instinctively avoid lying on cold/hard surfaces.

commonErrors.error: Skipping “sit” as the foundation
commonErrors.cause: Wanting shortcuts
commonErrors.fix: Fluent “sit” is a prerequisite. If not mastered, don't ask for down yet.

troubleshooting.problem: Follows the treat with nose but doesn't lower body
troubleshooting.solution: You're moving the treat too fast or too far. Keep it stuck to the floor and move very slowly forward.

troubleshooting.problem: Lies down but stands up immediately
troubleshooting.solution: Normal at first. Reward faster (within 1 second) and gradually increase duration.

troubleshooting.problem: Does a “sphinx” pose but doesn't lie laterally
troubleshooting.solution: Sphinx is valid and sufficient. Lateral form is more relaxed but not required for the basic command.

troubleshooting.problem: My large/old dog resists
troubleshooting.solution: May be joint pain. Consult the vet. Meanwhile, use a very padded surface.

progressMilestones.goal: Follows treat to the floor and bends front legs
Fully lies down with the lure 60% of attempts
Lies down on “down” command without needing the lure
Holds the position 30 seconds before reward

successSigns: Lies down on command with no visible lure
Does it in different places and positions
Holds the position more than 10 seconds
Returns to lying if they break the position when asked again
variations: Down at distance (1–2 meters away)
Full lateral down (on side, not sphinx)
Down during your breakfast while you eat
Down with only a downward hand gesture
Down after a chained sit (combining commands)
safetyNotes: If your dog shows pain or cracking when lying, consult the vet before continuing
Large breeds (Mastiffs, Great Danes) may take longer due to anatomy
Never force physically: it can create fear and command rejection
Puppies under 14 weeks: max 3 minutes per session
lie.funFact: Dogs only lie laterally (on their side) when they feel 100% safe. If yours does this with you, it's a sign of deep trust.
lie.nextLevel: Increase duration to 1–2 minutes. Practice with distractions and in public. Then introduce “stay”.
lie.proTip: If your dog won't lie, go back to “sit” and repeat slower. Always toss the treat to the floor between paws, never hand-feed: this reinforces staying down.

name.title: Respond to their name
name.subtitle: The foundation of all communication with your dog
name.location: Home with no distractions → garden → outside
name.objective: Get the dog to look at the handler immediately when they hear their name, in any context.
why: Without a response to the name you can't teach anything else
Necessary to control the dog on the street
Reinforces the bond and mutual attention
Foundation for recall and all distance commands
benefits: Your dog will come when called in parks or at friends' homes
Reduces accidents: turning to their name avoids dangers (cars, other dogs)
Essential for a reliable emergency recall
Builds a dog focused on you, not the environment
where: 🏠 At home, in a quiet room (sessions 1–3)
🛋️ Different rooms (sessions 4–6)
🌿 Garden or terrace (session 7+)
🌳 Outside with low distractions (empty park)
materials: 🫖 Very high-value treats (cheese, sausage, chicken)
🦮 Long leash 5–10 m (for outside)
🔇 Quiet environment at first
💛 Cheerful and enthusiastic voice
beforeYouStart: Make sure you haven't used the name as a reprimand previously
If the dog has negative associations with their name, consider changing it
Highest-value treats: no kibble here
Short sessions: 3–5 minutes, several times a day
Never use the name followed by something unpleasant (bath, nail trimming)

methods.title: The name game (classic)
methods.description: Repeatedly associate the name with something extremely positive.
methods.bestFor: Any dog, especially puppies and recently adopted dogs

steps.title: Capture mutual attention
steps.description: Sit on the floor in a quiet room. Wait until your dog is relaxed but not asleep.
steps.tip: Don't talk to or look at them at first.

steps.title: Say their name ONCE
steps.description: With a happy, soft voice, say their name clearly. Just once.
steps.tip: The tone should sound exciting, not commanding.
steps.troubleshooting: If they don't react, do NOT repeat the name: move to step 3.

steps.title: Reward immediately
steps.description: As soon as they look at you (even for a microsecond!), say “good!” and give a high-value treat.
steps.tip: If they don't look in 2 seconds, make a sound (click) to get attention and reward when they look.

steps.title: Space out the rewards
steps.description: Don't give another treat until you say the name again. Wait 10–30 seconds between repetitions.
steps.tip: If you do them back-to-back, the dog will start looking without your name.

steps.title: Change rooms
steps.description: After 5 successful sessions in the same room, move to another. Repeat the whole process.
steps.tip: Context change is where real learning happens.

steps.title: Level up: distractions
steps.description: Once it works in the whole house, try with TV on, other people present, food nearby.
steps.tip: Each new context = start with easy rewards.

commonErrors.error: Repeating the name multiple times (“Toby, Toby, Toby”)
commonErrors.cause: Frustration when they don't respond
commonErrors.fix: If no response first try, do NOT repeat. Get attention with a sound and reward when they look. Next time say the name from closer.

commonErrors.error: Using the name before something bad (bath, vet trip)
commonErrors.cause: Unconscious habit
commonErrors.fix: For unpleasant things, go get them physically without saying their name. The name must ALWAYS be positive.

commonErrors.error: Low-quality treats (dry kibble)
commonErrors.cause: Convenience
commonErrors.fix: Use the TASTIEST treats you have for teaching the name. It's an initial investment.

commonErrors.error: 30-minute sessions
commonErrors.cause: Thinking “more is better”
commonErrors.fix: Max 3–5 minutes. Dog focus runs out fast. Better 5 short sessions than 1 long one.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog has a long name and doesn't react
troubleshooting.solution: Use a short 1–2 syllable nickname for training. E.g. “Maximilian” → “Max”. Always keep the same.

troubleshooting.problem: Works at home but ignores me on the street
troubleshooting.solution: You need a long leash + VERY high treats. Start in empty areas. The street is “expert level” compared to home.

troubleshooting.problem: Looks at me but doesn't come closer
troubleshooting.solution: That's success in this course. Coming closer is the next level: the “Recall” course.

troubleshooting.problem: I have several dogs and don't know which to call
troubleshooting.solution: Train each in separate sessions first. Then use clearly distinct names by syllables.

progressMilestones.goal: Looks when hearing their name in a quiet room
Immediate reaction (under 1 second) in different rooms
Responds to name in garden with low distractions
Responds in park with other dogs and people 5 meters away

successSigns: Turns head immediately upon hearing their name
Does it without a visible treat
Works even with medium distractions (other dogs at distance)
Holds eye contact for a few seconds awaiting instructions
variations: Say the name from different sides (must turn looking for you)
Say the name when distracted sniffing
Say the name from another room (must come or look in)
Say the name when playing with other dogs
Combine name + silent gesture (clap hands)
safetyNotes: NEVER use the name in a scolding tone: you'd ruin months of work
If you're going to do something unpleasant, do it without naming the dog
Dogs with partial deafness: also use visual gestures and floor vibrations
If the dog was verbally abused, consider a new name and start from scratch
name.funFact: Dogs distinguish their name from other human words in just 2 weeks of consistent exposure. But they can forget it if it gets associated with negative things in only 3-4 episodes.
name.nextLevel: Move to the “Recall (come)” course: not just looking, but actually coming to you.
name.proTip: To keep the name “fresh” throughout the dog's life, keep rewarding occasionally when they respond — even years later. Once a month is enough to keep the response solid.

come.title: Recall (Come Here)
come.subtitle: The most important command for your dog's safety
come.location: Home, garden, or park with long leash
come.objective: Teach your dog to come immediately to your side when they hear their name followed by 'come' or 'here', even with distractions present.
why: It's the most critical safety command: it can save your dog's life
Allows you to give controlled freedom in open spaces
Strengthens the bond and trust between dog and handler
Foundation for distance work and off-leash exercises
benefits: You can let your dog off-leash in the park with confidence
In case of danger, your dog will return to you immediately
Makes it easy to call them away from other dogs or people
Improves overall communication and attention toward you
where: 🏠 Indoors (hallway or living room with no distractions)
🌿 Fenced garden or yard
🌳 Quiet park with a 5–10 metre long leash
materials: 🫖 Very high-value treats (chicken, cheese, ham in small pieces)
🦮 Long leash 5–10 metres (not retractable)
🔔 Clicker (optional but very helpful)
💛 Upbeat, enthusiastic tone of voice
beforeYouStart: Your dog should already respond to their name with some consistency
Never use the recall for unpleasant things (bath, nail trimming, being locked up)
Always use a celebratory tone: coming to you must feel like the best thing in the world
Start indoors or in a fenced garden, never in an open unfenced area
Keep high-value treats specifically reserved for this exercise

methods.title: Progressive recall game (recommended)
methods.description: You practise the recall as a game, starting very close and gradually increasing distance and difficulty. The dog learns that coming to you always produces the best reward.
methods.bestFor: All dogs from puppies to adults

steps.title: Start one metre away
steps.description: Crouch down to your dog's level, say their name and 'come' in a happy voice, and open your arms wide. When they arrive, give several treats in a row plus enthusiastic praise.
steps.tip: Crouching and opening your arms is an irresistible invitation for your dog.
steps.troubleshooting: If they don't come, move closer. Start at half a metre if needed.

steps.title: Increase distance gradually
steps.description: When they respond well at 1 metre, move to 2, then 3, then 5. Each time they come: big celebration — several treats, petting, and a very cheerful voice.
steps.tip: Golden rule: if they don't come 90% of the time, the distance is too great. Step back.
steps.troubleshooting: Never repeat the cue if they don't come. Move closer, show the treat, and try again at a shorter distance.

steps.title: Introduce the long leash
steps.description: In the garden or park with a 5–10 metre long leash. Let them explore, then call them during moderate distraction. When they come: total party.
steps.tip: The long leash is for safety, not to drag them in. Never use it to pull if they don't come.
steps.troubleshooting: If they're very distracted, wait for the distraction to decrease before calling.

steps.title: Alternate recall with freedom
steps.description: Call them, reward generously, and release them to keep exploring. This teaches them that coming to you does not mean the fun ends.
steps.tip: If you only call them when it's time to go home, they'll learn to ignore you at the end of a walk.

steps.title: Add progressive distractions
steps.description: Once they respond well in a quiet area, practise with other people, distant dogs, or sounds. Increase treat value as difficulty increases.
steps.tip: More distraction = bigger celebration when they arrive. Extra effort deserves extra reward.

commonErrors.error: Calling the dog for something unpleasant (bath, nail clipping, being shut in)
commonErrors.cause: We use the recall for necessary but unpleasant situations
commonErrors.fix: Go to them for unpleasant things. The recall MUST always end in something positive.

commonErrors.error: Scolding the dog when they finally come (even if they took a long time)
commonErrors.cause: Frustration over the delay
commonErrors.fix: Never. Even if they take 10 minutes, when they arrive: celebrate. Punishing the arrival means they'll never come back.

commonErrors.error: Repeating the cue multiple times ('come, come, come…')
commonErrors.cause: Nervousness or lack of patience
commonErrors.fix: Say the cue ONCE in a happy tone. If they don't come, move closer and try again at a shorter distance next time.

commonErrors.error: Only practising at home where it always works
commonErrors.cause: Handler's comfort zone
commonErrors.fix: Practise in new places with real distractions. Learning must generalise to different environments.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog looks at me but doesn't come
troubleshooting.solution: The treats aren't attractive enough. Use chicken or cheese and exaggerate your enthusiasm: crouch, clap, very happy voice.

troubleshooting.problem: They come but run away before I can reach them
troubleshooting.solution: You're grabbing their collar too quickly. Reward first for 3 seconds, then gently hold the collar while continuing to treat.

troubleshooting.problem: It works at home but in the park they ignore me
troubleshooting.solution: Normal: the park has too many distractions. Start in the park when it's empty and increase difficulty very slowly.

troubleshooting.problem: They've stopped responding even though they used to do it well
troubleshooting.solution: You may have increased difficulty too fast, or used the recall for something negative. Go back to short distances with excellent treats for a week.

progressMilestones.goal: Comes consistently from 1–3 metres indoors with no distractions
Responds from 5 metres in the garden with mild distractions
Comes from 10 metres on a long leash in a quiet park
Responds in environments with real distractions (other dogs, people)

successSigns: Comes on the first call without needing the cue repeated
Abandons moderate distractions (sniffing, exploring) to come to you
Arrives fully at your side and stays (not just approaches)
Responds in at least 3 different environments
variations: Recall between two people (dog goes back and forth)
Recall when you're hidden behind a tree or around a corner
Recall during play with another dog
Recall with hand signal only (no voice)
Long-distance recall from 20–30 metres
safetyNotes: Never practise off-leash in open areas until the recall is very solid
Avoid practising when the dog is highly excited: wait for their arousal level to drop
If using a long leash, check it's not tangled before calling
Save an emergency recall (loud, dramatic voice) for real danger only — use it rarely so it keeps its impact
come.funFact: Studies show dogs respond better to high-pitched, happy voices than deep, serious tones. The sillier you sound calling them, the better it works!
come.nextLevel: Practise recall with real distractions: dogs playing nearby, people running, strong smells. Then introduce a stay before calling them.
come.proTip: Reserve your best treats ONLY for the recall. If chicken only appears when they come to you, they'll come flying. Exclusivity makes the behaviour stronger.

stay.title: Stay
stay.subtitle: Build impulse control: your dog learns to wait in position
stay.objective: Teach your dog to hold a position (sit or down) until they receive a release cue, gradually increasing duration, distance, and distractions.
why: Builds self-control and impulse management — key skills for everyday life
Allows safe handling in daily situations (crossing the street, front door)
Essential companion to 'sit' and 'down' to make those commands more useful
Reduces hyperactivity and impulsiveness in the dog
benefits: Your dog waits calmly while you prepare their food or open the door
Can hold a stay at restaurant terraces or at the vet
Prevents dangerous escapes through the front door
Makes handling easier in situations with people, cars, or bicycles
where: 🏠 Indoors (living room or hallway with no distractions)
🌿 Quiet garden once consolidated indoors
⛔ Never in an open area without safety until it's very solid
materials: 🫖 Small, soft, high-value treats
🦮 Short leash (optional for very active dogs)
🛏️ Mat or blanket as a position reference
💛 Patience: this exercise takes more time than others
beforeYouStart: Your dog must have a fluent sit or down before you begin
Choose a clear release word: 'ok', 'free', or 'go' and use it consistently
Start with only 1 second of duration: early success is key
Never increase distance and duration at the same time
Always end the session with a stay your dog achieves perfectly

methods.title: 3D Progression (recommended)
methods.description: You work on the three dimensions of 'stay' separately and in order: first Duration, then Distance, and finally Distractions. Mixing them too soon is the most common mistake.
methods.bestFor: All dogs that already know sit or down

steps.title: Phase 1 – Duration (without moving)
steps.description: Ask for 'sit' or 'down', say 'stay' calmly, and wait 1 second before rewarding. Then release with 'ok'. Build from 1 to 3, 5, 10, 30 seconds gradually.
steps.tip: If they break position, don't scold. Simply ask for the position again and reduce the duration.
steps.troubleshooting: If they can't hold for more than 1 second, reward at 0.5 seconds and build very slowly.

steps.title: Phase 2 – Distance (once they hold 30 seconds without you moving)
steps.description: Take one step back while your dog is in 'stay'. Return before they move and reward. Build to 2, 3, 5 steps gradually.
steps.tip: Always go BACK to reward beside the dog. Don't call them — go to them.
steps.troubleshooting: If they stand up when you move away, reduce the distance. One step is enough at first.

steps.title: Phase 3 – Combine duration and distance
steps.description: Once they hold for 5 steps without moving, start combining: step back and also wait a few seconds before returning to reward.
steps.tip: The rule: if they fail, simplify. Go back to what was working.

steps.title: Phase 4 – Mild distractions
steps.description: With your dog in 'stay', introduce small distractions: drop something, move sideways, clap softly. If they hold, reward generously.
steps.tip: The stronger the distraction, the bigger the reward for holding the stay.
steps.troubleshooting: If the distraction is too much and they break, go back to a milder one.

steps.title: Release cue
steps.description: Always end 'stay' with your release word ('ok', 'free'). Your dog learns they can only move when you signal, not whenever they feel like it.
steps.tip: The release is as important as the stay itself. Teach it from day one.

commonErrors.error: Increasing duration and distance at the same time
commonErrors.cause: Wanting to progress too quickly
commonErrors.fix: Work one dimension at a time. More distance = less duration. More duration = less distance.

commonErrors.error: Calling the dog from a distance to end the stay
commonErrors.cause: Handler convenience
commonErrors.fix: Always go back to reward beside them. Calling from a distance trains the recall, not the stay.

commonErrors.error: Not using a release word
commonErrors.cause: Oversight or unawareness
commonErrors.fix: Without a release cue, the dog decides when to move. Set 'ok' or 'free' from day one.

commonErrors.error: Scolding the dog when they break position
commonErrors.cause: Frustration
commonErrors.fix: Simply ask for the position again. Breaking indicates the exercise was too hard, not that the dog is disobedient.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog moves as soon as I take one step back
troubleshooting.solution: Distance came too soon. Go back to phase 1 (duration only, without moving) until they hold comfortably for 30 seconds.

troubleshooting.problem: They hold the stay indoors but not on the street
troubleshooting.solution: Normal: outdoor distractions are stronger. Start again from 1 second in the new environment.

troubleshooting.problem: They get up right as I'm about to reward them
troubleshooting.solution: Your hand moving toward the treat pocket is their signal to get up. Vary the timing of when you reach for the treat.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog stays but looks very anxious
troubleshooting.solution: Greatly reduce duration and distance. The stay should be comfortable, not stressful. Anxiety means the exercise is too demanding.

progressMilestones.goal: Holds sit or down for 5–10 seconds without you moving
Holds position with 3–5 steps of distance for 10 seconds
Holds for 30 seconds with 5 steps distance indoors
Maintains stay with mild distractions (noises, lateral movements)

successSigns: Holds position until they hear the release word
Doesn't move when you step 5 or more paces away
Maintains position with small distractions nearby
The stay works in both sit and down positions
variations: Stay while you open and close the front door
Stay while you prepare their meal (impulse control)
Stay while other people walk nearby
Stay while you crouch down or sit on the floor
Stay outdoors in a fenced area
safetyNotes: Never use 'stay' to leave the dog alone in a risky area (open street, balcony)
If your dog becomes very stressed during the exercise, take a break and simplify
Very active or anxious dogs need more time — don't compare them to others
Puppies under 14 weeks: maximum 3 minutes per session
stay.funFact: German Shepherds and Border Collies learn 'stay' in just a few sessions, but terriers and spaniels may need twice as long due to their naturally high impulsiveness. Breed matters!
stay.nextLevel: Practise 'stay' with real distractions: other dogs, bicycles, people running. Then combine it with 'place' so your dog goes and stays in a specific spot.
stay.proTip: A stay breaks down when the dog loses motivation or the environment is too challenging. If they fail three times in a row, the exercise is too hard — step back one level and end on a success.

leash.title: Loose-leash walking
leash.subtitle: Enjoyable walks for both you and your dog — no more pulling
leash.objective: Teach your dog to walk beside you without tightening the leash, using the tree method and direction changes with positive reinforcement.
why: A dog that pulls makes walks exhausting and dangerous for the handler
Constant leash tension can injure the dog's neck and trachea
Loose-leash walking improves the relationship and mutual trust
Foundation for advancing to off-leash work in safe spaces
benefits: Walks become relaxing and enjoyable for the whole family
Reduces the risk of falls or injuries, especially with large dogs
Your dog learns to pay attention to you during walks
Improves overall management of the dog in public spaces
where: 🏠 Start at home or in the garden before heading outside
🛣️ A quiet street with few distractions at first
🌳 A quiet park once steady progress has been made
materials: 🦮 H or Y-harness (NOT a prong, choke, or electric collar)
📏 Fixed leash 1.5–2 metres (NOT retractable)
🫖 High-value treats in an easily accessible pocket
💛 Patience: this is a process, not an instant fix
beforeYouStart: Always use a front-clip H or Y harness: distributes pressure and protects the neck
NEVER use a prong collar, choke chain, electric collar, or slip lead
A retractable leash won't work for this exercise: it can't give clear signals
Start sessions when your dog's energy is lower (after play)
Keep treats on hand at all times during training

methods.title: Tree method + direction changes (recommended)
methods.description: When the dog pulls, you stop like a tree until the leash goes slack. When the leash is loose, you move forward. You change direction randomly to keep their attention on you.
methods.bestFor: All dogs, especially those that already have a pulling habit

steps.title: Starting position and start cue
steps.description: Dog at your side (left or right — pick one and stay consistent). Say 'let's go' or 'walk' as a start cue and begin walking.
steps.tip: Always use the same side. Consistency is key for your dog to understand what's expected.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog bolts and pulls from the very first step, stop like a tree before you've even taken one pace.

steps.title: Tree: stop when they pull
steps.description: The moment the leash tightens, stop completely. No jerking, no shouting, no movement. Wait in silence until the leash goes slack.
steps.tip: The stop must be immediate: any delay confuses the dog.
steps.troubleshooting: If they don't release the leash, take one step toward them (no jerking) to create slack, then wait for them to follow.

steps.title: Reward the loose leash
steps.description: The instant the leash goes slack (dog looks at you, moves closer, or simply steps back), say 'yes' in a cheerful voice and reward. Then keep walking.
steps.tip: Reward the exact moment the leash goes slack, not five seconds later.

steps.title: Change direction
steps.description: Randomly, without warning, turn around and walk the other way. When the dog follows and catches up with a loose leash, reward generously.
steps.tip: Frequent direction changes teach the dog you are unpredictable and they need to stay attentive to you.
steps.troubleshooting: Don't worry if you seem to be going in circles at first. That's normal and necessary.

steps.title: Proactively reward attention
steps.description: Whenever your dog looks up at you during the walk (without being asked), reward immediately. This reinforces that looking at you is a very rewarding option.
steps.tip: A voluntary check-in is the best sign the exercise is working.

commonErrors.error: Using a collar instead of a harness
commonErrors.cause: Habit or not knowing the damage it causes
commonErrors.fix: A collar with a pulling dog can cause tracheal, vertebral, or thyroid damage. Switch to an H or Y harness immediately.

commonErrors.error: Giving in and walking on when the dog pulls
commonErrors.cause: Tiredness or wanting to reach a destination
commonErrors.fix: Every time you advance while they pull, you reinforce the pulling. Consistency is non-negotiable.

commonErrors.error: Jerking the leash backward to correct
commonErrors.cause: Instinctive reaction
commonErrors.fix: Jerks create opposition reflex (the dog pulls harder). Stop without moving and wait in silence.

commonErrors.error: Sessions too long in a very stimulating environment
commonErrors.cause: Wanting to progress quickly in difficult settings
commonErrors.fix: Start with 5–10 minutes on a quiet street. Only increase when the dog is consistently doing well.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog pulls from the very second we step outside
troubleshooting.solution: The excitement threshold is very high at departure. Practise first in the hallway or building entrance. Once calm there, step outside.

troubleshooting.problem: I stop like a tree but the dog never slackens the leash
troubleshooting.solution: Take a step toward the dog to create some slack, wait for them to look at you, and reward. Then resume walking.

troubleshooting.problem: It works well on quiet streets but with other dogs they pull like crazy
troubleshooting.solution: Other dogs are advanced-level distractions. Increase your distance from other dogs until you can reward a loose leash, then very slowly reduce that distance.

troubleshooting.problem: The dog seems to understand but seems to forget by the next day
troubleshooting.solution: Normal in the first weeks. Daily consistency beats occasional long sessions. 10 minutes every day outperforms 1 hour on Saturdays.

progressMilestones.goal: Dog associates leash tension with stopping. Stops at least 50% of the time
Walks 10–20 steps continuously with a loose leash on a quiet street
Offers voluntary check-ins (looks at you) during the walk without being asked
Maintains a loose leash in moderately stimulating environments (park, busy street)

successSigns: The leash has a relaxed U-shape for most of the walk
The dog looks up at you spontaneously without being asked
Stops next to you without pulling when you stop
Recovers a loose leash within 2–3 seconds after a distraction
variations: Walk with frequent turns in a training area
Formal 'heel': dog pressed close to your left leg
Stop-and-go: pause 3 seconds every 10 steps and reward if they don't forge ahead
Walk with another person: dog learns to ignore the second human
Walk with a dog backpack (naturally increases focus)
safetyNotes: NEVER use a choke chain, prong collar, or electric collar: they cause pain and physical and behavioural damage
If your dog has neck or trachea issues, consult your vet before starting
On very hot days, limit sessions to 5 minutes and avoid hot asphalt
Highly reactive dogs (barking or lunging at other dogs): seek professional help before working in the street
leash.funFact: Dogs pull because walking fast toward interesting things has worked their entire life. It's not dominance or bad behaviour — it's simply what has always paid off for them. Now we're teaching them that a loose leash works even better!
leash.nextLevel: Practise in more stimulating environments: markets, busy parks, areas with other dogs. Then introduce formal heel work for more precise walking at your side.
leash.proTip: When your dog offers a voluntary check-in (looks at you unprompted during the walk), reward them like they've just won the lottery. That spontaneous moment of attention is what turns a walk into true teamwork.

paw.title: Shake / Give Paw
paw.subtitle: The classic trick that strengthens the bond and makes grooming easier
paw.objective: Teach the dog to lift a front paw and place it in the handler's hand on the cue "shake" or "give paw".
why: Makes nail trims and vet check-ups much easier
Strengthens the bond between dog and handler
Develops the dog's body awareness
Foundation for advanced tricks like high-five or wave
benefits: Your dog will be calmer at the vet and during grooming
Builds mutual trust through playful interaction
Improves coordination and balance
A crowd-pleasing trick the whole family will enjoy
where: 🏠 At home on a non-slip surface
🌿 In the garden on grass or firm ground
🔇 Distraction-free environment at first
materials: 🫖 High-value treats (chicken, cheese, soft jerky)
🛏️ Non-slip mat or carpet
✋ Your open hand as the target
💛 Patience and short sessions
beforeYouStart: Your dog must know "sit" reliably before starting
Choose high-motivation treats — this trick demands something special
Make sure the surface is non-slip so your dog feels secure
Keep sessions to 5 minutes max to avoid mental fatigue
Start with the same paw every time (right paw is common)

methods.title: Capture with gentle shoulder prompt (recommended)
methods.description: You wait for the dog to naturally lift a paw from the sitting position, helped by a light shoulder tap, and reward that movement.
methods.bestFor: Puppies and dogs of any size that already know sit

steps.title: Ask for sit and present your hand
steps.description: Ask your dog to sit. Extend your open hand, palm up, at chest height. Say nothing else — just wait.
steps.tip: Your open hand is the visual cue. Keep a relaxed, expectant posture.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog ignores your hand, bring it slightly closer to the paws without touching.

steps.title: Gentle shoulder tap
steps.description: If the dog hasn't lifted the paw after 5 seconds, lightly graze the shoulder or outer leg with one finger. Most dogs will lift the paw instinctively.
steps.tip: The tap should feel like a tickle — not a push or push.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog stands up, ask for sit again calmly and start over.

steps.title: Capture the movement and reward
steps.description: The exact moment the paw lifts off the ground and touches your hand, say "yes!" in a happy voice and deliver the treat instantly.
steps.tip: Timing is everything. Reward the paw touching your hand, not before or after.
steps.troubleshooting: If the paw doesn't reach your hand, first reward any paw lift at all, then gradually require more.

steps.title: Add the verbal cue
steps.description: Once the dog lifts the paw consistently (7 out of 10 times), add the word "shake" just before extending your hand.
steps.tip: Gesture first, word second. Don't add the word until the behavior is reliable.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog looks confused, drop the word for 2 sessions and go back to just the gesture.

steps.title: Fade the tap and extend duration
steps.description: Gradually stop using the shoulder tap. Then begin gently closing your hand around the paw and holding for 2–3 seconds before rewarding.
steps.tip: The end goal is the dog keeping the paw in your hand until you release it.
steps.troubleshooting: If the paw is pulled away quickly, reward more frequently and increase time very gradually.

commonErrors.error: Grabbing the paw by force
commonErrors.cause: Impatience when the dog doesn't understand what's being asked
commonErrors.fix: Never take the paw without the dog offering it. Use the gentle tap and wait.

commonErrors.error: Rewarding after the paw is already on the way down
commonErrors.cause: Slow reward timing
commonErrors.fix: Practice your timing alone: toss a treat in the air and catch it in under 1 second.

commonErrors.error: Switching paws on every attempt
commonErrors.cause: Inconsistency from the handler
commonErrors.fix: Work the same paw for the first few weeks. Introduce the other paw later.

commonErrors.error: Cueing the trick without the dog in a sit
commonErrors.cause: Skipping steps in the learning process
commonErrors.fix: A solid sit is required for this trick. Always start from there.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog won't lift the paw even after waiting a long time
troubleshooting.solution: Try holding a treat in a closed fist in front of their chest. Many dogs paw at the fist to open it.

troubleshooting.problem: Dog lifts the paw but doesn't place it in my hand
troubleshooting.solution: Move your hand closer to the paws. The correct distance is almost effortless contact.

troubleshooting.problem: Works at home but not outside
troubleshooting.solution: Normal. Practice first in the garden, then on a quiet street. Use higher-value treats in new environments.

troubleshooting.problem: Dog confuses "shake" with "sit"
troubleshooting.solution: Differentiate the hand signal: for sit point downward; for shake, hold your palm flat and horizontal.

progressMilestones.goal: Dog lifts the paw even just a centimeter when seeing your hand or feeling the tap
Places paw in your open hand at least 6 out of 10 times
Responds to the verbal cue "shake" without needing the shoulder tap
Holds the paw in your hand for 3–5 seconds until you release it

successSigns: Lifts the paw as soon as the cue is given
Places the paw gently without scratching
Stays in a sit while offering the paw
Performs in different locations and with different people
variations: Left paw shake (teach the other paw)
High-five (paw raised higher, vertical palm)
Shake on hand gesture only, no verbal cue
Shake while handler is crouching or standing
Chain: sit → shake → stay
safetyNotes: Stop if your dog shows pain when lifting the paw — this may indicate a joint problem
Large breeds or dogs with hip dysplasia: shorter sessions on very soft surfaces
Never punish failure; simply go back to the previous step
Puppies under 16 weeks have developing bones — never force postures
paw.funFact: The "give paw" trick is one of the oldest on record — European engravings from the 17th century depict dogs greeting their owners this way.
paw.nextLevel: Teach the left paw so the dog learns to distinguish both. Then build toward high-five by gradually raising your palm higher.
paw.proTip: If your dog is hand-shy, start with a closed fist holding a treat. The dog will stop seeing your hand as a threat and start seeing it as a vending machine.

place.title: Go to Your Place
place.subtitle: Your dog learns to go to their mat and stay until you release them
place.location: Home with a designated mat or bed
place.objective: Teach the dog to go to a designated mat or bed and remain calmly there until given a release cue.
why: Gives the dog their own safe space in the home
Reduces intrusive behavior during meals or when guests arrive
Teaches the dog to self-settle
Lays the foundation for distraction management at home
benefits: Your dog won't bother you during meals or when guests come over
Reduces anxiety by providing a predictable, safe space
Improves self-control and frustration tolerance
Allows the dog to rest without being constantly underfoot
where: 🏠 At home, with the mat always in the same spot
🛋️ In the living room or main family activity area
⛔ Avoid high-traffic areas where the dog will be disturbed
materials: 🛏️ A designated bed, blanket or mat (always the same one)
🫖 High-value treats for the first sessions
🦮 Long leash (optional, for early distance work)
💛 Patience and daily consistency
beforeYouStart: Your dog should have a solid "down" and "stay" before starting
Choose one spot for the mat and don't change it during training
The bed must be comfortable and large enough to lie down fully
Have high-value treats ready: this exercise demands more focus
Practice in calm moments, not when the dog is already excited

methods.title: Lure-to-mat method (recommended)
methods.description: You use a treat to guide the dog to the mat, then progressively add distance, duration, and distractions.
methods.bestFor: Dogs that already know down and stay

steps.title: Lure the dog onto the mat
steps.description: With a treat in your hand, guide the dog toward the mat. When all four paws are on it, say "place" and deliver the treat.
steps.tip: Drop the treat on the mat, not on the floor. This reinforces being on the mat.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog won't step on the mat, start with the treat at the edge, then gradually move it to the center.

steps.title: Ask for a down on the mat
steps.description: Once on the mat, ask for "down". When the dog lies down, reward. The goal is now lying down on their place.
steps.tip: The down position makes it much easier to maintain calm and build duration.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog won't lie down, use the same lure technique from the down course.

steps.title: Introduce the release word
steps.description: After 2–3 seconds of lying down, say "free" (or "okay" — always the same word) and encourage the dog off the mat. Do not reward outside the mat at this stage.
steps.tip: The release word is as important as the command itself. Without it, the dog doesn't know when they can leave.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog leaves before being released, calmly return them to the mat without scolding.

steps.title: Add distance
steps.description: Once the dog goes to the mat and lies down consistently, start stepping back one step, then two, then three. Return before the dog moves and reward on the mat.
steps.tip: Always walk back to the dog — never call them to you. This reinforces staying, not coming.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog follows you, reduce to half a step and practice that level many times.

steps.title: Add duration and distractions
steps.description: Build time progressively (5s → 15s → 30s → 1 min). Then introduce small distractions: moving around the room, opening the fridge, knocking on the door.
steps.tip: Increase distance OR duration OR distraction — never all three at once.
steps.troubleshooting: If the exercise falls apart, always simplify: reduce whichever variable you just increased.

commonErrors.error: Calling the dog away from their place instead of going back to them
commonErrors.cause: Confusing "stay on mat" with "come when called"
commonErrors.fix: Always walk back to the dog to reward and release. This reinforces staying on the mat.

commonErrors.error: Increasing difficulty too fast
commonErrors.cause: Overconfidence after early successes
commonErrors.fix: Follow the 80% rule: only increase difficulty when the dog succeeds 8 out of 10 times.

commonErrors.error: Moving or changing the mat frequently
commonErrors.cause: Lack of environmental planning
commonErrors.fix: The mat location should be consistent during training. Environmental stability supports learning.

commonErrors.error: Scolding the dog when they leave the mat
commonErrors.cause: Handler frustration
commonErrors.fix: Simply return the dog to the mat in silence. Going back should never be a negative experience.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog goes to the mat but leaves after a few seconds
troubleshooting.solution: You're waiting too long before rewarding. Reward every 1–2 seconds initially to reinforce being on the mat.

troubleshooting.problem: The dog won't step onto the mat at all
troubleshooting.solution: Make the mat more appealing: put their favorite blanket, a toy, or give their best treats there for several days before training.

troubleshooting.problem: Goes to the mat but won't lie down
troubleshooting.solution: Practice "down" on the mat as a separate exercise before introducing distance.

troubleshooting.problem: Works at home but not at friends' houses or on trips
troubleshooting.solution: Always bring the same mat or portable blanket. The familiar scent serves as a contextual cue for the dog.

progressMilestones.goal: Dog goes to the mat with a lure and lies down when asked
Goes to the mat on the verbal cue and stays for 15 seconds
Stays on the mat while you move 3 meters away for 30 seconds
Remains on the mat for 2–5 minutes with mild distractions (doorbell, movement in room)

successSigns: Goes to the mat on cue without a lure
Lies down and stays until hearing the release word
Doesn't move even when you step away or briefly leave the room
Voluntarily uses the mat to rest without being asked
variations: Place in different rooms of the house
Place at relatives' or friends' homes (same mat)
Place during a full family dinner
Place while receiving guests
Place in the garden or on the patio
safetyNotes: Never use the mat as punishment: it must always be a positive place
Make sure the bed is large enough for the dog to be comfortable
Do not expect very long stays initially — build duration gradually
If the dog seems anxious on the mat, check whether the spot is too isolated
place.funFact: Dogs that have a well-established place of their own show significantly lower cortisol (stress hormone) levels than dogs that roam freely without a defined space.
place.nextLevel: Practice "place" with the front door opening, guests entering, and finally in pet-friendly public spaces with a portable mat.
place.proTip: Feed your dog on their mat for one week before starting training. This way, the mat becomes the best place in the world before you even start asking for anything.

distraction.title: Focus Under Distraction
distraction.subtitle: Your dog stays attentive to you even when the whole world calls their name
distraction.objective: Teach the dog to maintain attention and obedience even when distractions appear — other dogs, people, food on the ground, or loud noises.
why: Attention is the foundation of all real-world obedience
A dog that looks at you on cue is a safe and manageable dog
Prevents accidents on the street and dangerous situations
Reduces reactivity and over-excitement in new environments
benefits: You'll be able to walk calmly even when other dogs are nearby
Your dog won't lunge at dropped food on the street
They'll respond to commands even at the park or friends' homes
Reduces your dog's anxiety in unfamiliar environments
where: 🏠 Always start at home with no distractions
🌿 Progress to the garden, then a quiet street
🎯 Finish in the park or environments with real distractions
materials: 🫖 Maximum-motivation treats (cooked chicken, cheese, sausage)
🦮 2-meter leash for outdoor phases
🎯 Your voice, gaze, and body language as your main tools
💛 Patience to progress very slowly at first
beforeYouStart: Your dog must have solid "stay" and "come" at home with no distractions
Always start with very small distractions — never the hardest level first
Use top-quality treats: they need to compete with whatever is distracting your dog
Keep sessions to 5 minutes: focused attention under pressure is mentally exhausting
Expect regressions and bad days. Consistency is what fixes them

methods.title: Gradient method with "watch me" cue (recommended)
methods.description: You build focus gradually: first in a neutral setting, then with progressively more intense distractions. The "watch me" cue teaches the dog to look to you when something interesting appears.
methods.bestFor: Dogs with high arousal or dogs that get locked onto stimuli

steps.title: Teach "watch me" without distractions
steps.description: At home, hold a treat near your eye and wait. The moment the dog makes eye contact, say "watch me", reward, and praise. Repeat 10 times per session.
steps.tip: You won't need to hold the treat near your eye later — just say the word and wait for eye contact.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog looks at the treat but not your eyes, slowly move the treat up toward your forehead.

steps.title: Introduce a very small distraction
steps.description: Place a boring toy or neutral object 3 meters away. Cue "watch me". If they look at you, reward generously. If not, increase distance to the distraction only if the dog looks well from far away.
steps.tip: The distraction should be interesting but not irresistible. If the dog can't ignore it, it's too much.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog can't look away, move the distraction farther away or use a less interesting one.

steps.title: Practice with moving distractions
steps.description: Now use distractions that move: a rolling ball, a person walking, a dog at a distance. Cue "watch me" just before the distraction appears or approaches.
steps.tip: The key moment is asking for attention BEFORE the dog notices the distraction, not after.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog is already locked on the distraction, step sideways or turn around to break their focus, then ask for attention.

steps.title: Add obedience under distraction
steps.description: Once the dog focuses reliably near distractions, combine "watch me" with "sit" or "stay". The dog should be able to follow commands even with something interesting nearby.
steps.tip: Reward success with a JACKPOT: 5–6 treats in a row when they obey with a distraction present.
steps.troubleshooting: If combined commands fail, go back to just "watch me" and increase difficulty more slowly.

steps.title: Generalize in real environments
steps.description: Take the training to the park, busy streets, markets. In each new environment, start with the smallest distractions and progress gradually.
steps.tip: Every new environment is like starting over: the dog needs an adjustment period.
steps.troubleshooting: If at the park focus is impossible, take a short walk first so the dog releases energy before training.

commonErrors.error: Starting with maximum distraction from day one
commonErrors.cause: Wanting quick results
commonErrors.fix: Always start below threshold: the level where the dog CAN ignore the distraction. Move up step by step.

commonErrors.error: Repeating the cue when the dog is locked onto the distraction
commonErrors.cause: Believing that repeating more times will work
commonErrors.fix: If the dog is locked on, change your own position (move laterally, walk away) then ask for attention.

commonErrors.error: Using low-value treats when distractions are strong
commonErrors.cause: Not calibrating treat value to exercise difficulty
commonErrors.fix: Higher distraction = higher treat value. Cooked chicken or cheese must beat whatever is distracting your dog.

commonErrors.error: Training when the dog is already over-stimulated
commonErrors.cause: Wrong timing (arriving at the park, after intense play)
commonErrors.fix: Wait 10–15 minutes after arriving in a new environment or after intense play. The mind settles with time.

troubleshooting.problem: At the park my dog ignores me completely
troubleshooting.solution: The distraction level is too high. Take a 10-minute walk first to lower arousal, then find a quiet corner of the park to start.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog gets locked looking at other dogs and doesn't react to anything
troubleshooting.solution: You are too close to the other dog. The safe distance is where your dog can still see you even with the distraction present. Increase distance.

troubleshooting.problem: Works great at home but on the street it's like they know nothing
troubleshooting.solution: Normal: dogs learn in context. Practice in the hallway, then at the front door, then 5 meters away, then the corner. Generalize in small steps.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog improves and then seems to go backwards
troubleshooting.solution: Regressions are normal, especially during growth phases or environmental changes. Go back one level and progress again.

progressMilestones.goal: Dog maintains eye contact with you for 3–5 seconds with small static distractions at home
Responds to "watch me" in the garden with people or dogs 10+ meters away
Can perform sit or stay on the street even as people or cyclists pass
Maintains focus at the park with other dogs in the environment, responding to basic commands

successSigns: Dog spontaneously looks at you when something interesting appears
Responds to basic commands even with moderate distractions
Can walk at your side without pulling even when other dogs are 5 meters away
Redirects attention toward you when asked, even at the park
variations: Focus with food on the ground (especially useful in cities)
Focus with other dogs running nearby
Focus with loud noises (fireworks, motorcycles, construction)
Focus while waiting at the vet
safetyNotes: Never put the dog in situations that far exceed their threshold: it can cause trauma or increase reactivity
If your dog shows fear signs (tucked tail, ears back, trembling), stop the session and increase distance from the distraction
Reactive dogs need professional help: the gradient method alone is not enough for severe cases
Do not train attention under distraction with a tight leash: it increases the dog's stress
distraction.funFact: Dogs process the world at up to 5 times the speed of humans. What seems like a minor distraction to you can be a full sensory avalanche for your dog.
distraction.nextLevel: Practice with very high-value distractions like food in another person's hand or dogs in free play. Then introduce "drop it" combined with attention work.
distraction.proTip: Become the most interesting thing on the walk: talk to your dog, change pace, make unexpected turns. An unpredictable, fun handler generates natural attention without having to ask for it.

drop.title: Drop It
drop.subtitle: The command that can save your dog's life
drop.objective: Teach the dog to immediately release any object — toy, food, dangerous item — on the cue "drop it", using the trade-up game as the foundation.
why: Can save the dog's life if they pick up something dangerous or toxic
Prevents chase games that reinforce holding on
Reduces resource guarding behavior (growling when you approach)
A safety skill every dog must know
benefits: You can safely retrieve any dangerous object from your dog's mouth
Fetch and retrieve games become much smoother and more fun
Reduces tension and conflict around valued objects
Builds trust: the dog learns that dropping always brings something good
where: 🏠 At home, always the first training environment
🌿 In the garden once solid at home
🎯 Any environment with real objects once generalized
materials: 🫖 Very high-value treats (chicken, cheese, sausage — the best you have)
🦴 A low-value toy to start (not the dog's favorite)
🦮 Optional leash for the first phase
💛 Complete calm — no anger or frustration ever
beforeYouStart: Your dog should have some impulse control from previous courses
Never attempt to pull an object from your dog's mouth by force
If your dog growls defensively over objects, consult a professional before continuing
Always have the trade (the treat) ready before approaching the dog
Accept that early on the dog may learn to drop quickly to get the treat before you even ask

methods.title: Trade-up method (recommended)
methods.description: You offer something of higher value than what the dog has in exchange for dropping it. You never snatch the object. The dog learns that dropping always means getting something better.
methods.bestFor: All dogs, especially those prone to resource guarding

steps.title: Start with a low-value toy
steps.description: Give the dog a toy they like moderately (not their favorite). Let them have it and enjoy it for a moment.
steps.tip: If there's no starting object, try one with treat scent or that has been rewarded near before.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog won't pick up the toy, try a more interesting one or play with it yourself for a few seconds first.

steps.title: Calmly approach with the treat visible
steps.description: Without rushing, walk toward the dog with the treat in your open hand, clearly visible. Don't try to take the toy yet — just let the dog see what you have.
steps.tip: Calm is key. If you approach fast or tensely, the dog will grip harder.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog moves away when you approach, practice walking toward and away without asking anything for several days first.

steps.title: Offer the trade — don't demand the object
steps.description: Bring the treat to the dog's nose while they hold the toy. When they open their mouth to sniff or take the treat, the toy will fall naturally. Say "drop it" at that exact moment.
steps.tip: The key: the toy falls because the dog opens their mouth for the treat. You don't pull it out.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog grips tighter, remove the treat, wait a few seconds, and try again more slowly.

steps.title: Reward generously and return the toy
steps.description: Give several treats in a row while the toy is on the floor. Then hand the toy back to the dog. This teaches that dropping is not permanent loss.
steps.tip: Returning the toy is essential: if you always keep it, the dog will learn to never drop it.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog doesn't want the toy back, that's fine. The trade was a success regardless.

steps.title: Generalize with more challenging objects
steps.description: Over time, practice "drop it" with favorite toys, found food, socks, or any object the dog picks up. For dangerous objects, the response must be automatic.
steps.tip: Always trade: even if you later let them keep the toy, the trade must happen first.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog learns to pick things up just to get the trade, also practice "leave it" (don't touch a specific object) as a complement.

commonErrors.error: Trying to pull the object out of the dog's mouth
commonErrors.cause: Instinct to solve the problem quickly
commonErrors.fix: Never put your hand in or pull. Always use the trade. Forcing can cause defensive biting.

commonErrors.error: Chasing the dog when they have something they shouldn't
commonErrors.cause: Panic at seeing the dangerous object
commonErrors.fix: Don't run after the dog. Sit on the floor, show the treat and wait. Chasing turns this into an irresistible game.

commonErrors.error: Never returning the toy after the trade
commonErrors.cause: Thinking "if they drop it, we take it"
commonErrors.fix: Always return the object when safe. The dog must learn that dropping is temporary and neutral, not a permanent loss.

commonErrors.error: Using low-value treats to trade for something highly prized
commonErrors.cause: Not calibrating the value of the trade
commonErrors.fix: The trade must always be "better". For the favorite toy, use the absolute best treat available.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog opens their mouth but takes a long time to drop
troubleshooting.solution: That is progress. Keep rewarding generously and response time will reduce with practice.

troubleshooting.problem: The dog growls when I approach to take the object
troubleshooting.solution: This is resource guarding: never force it. Consult a professional trainer. In the meantime, don't approach objects that cause tension.

troubleshooting.problem: Works fine with toys but not with food found on the ground
troubleshooting.solution: Food is extremely high value. Practice first with lower-value treats near the food, increasing the challenge very slowly.

troubleshooting.problem: Dog quickly learns to grab things just to get the trade
troubleshooting.solution: Sign of intelligence. Add "leave it" (don't touch a neutral object) as a complement so the dog learns both sides of the behavior.

progressMilestones.goal: Dog opens mouth and releases the toy when seeing the treat, even if it takes 3–5 seconds
Drops within 2 seconds of hearing "drop it" with medium-value toys
Drops immediately even with the favorite toy in exchange for the treat
Drops objects found on the street on hearing the cue, without you needing to show the treat first

successSigns: Releases the object on cue without needing to see the treat first
Does not growl or move away when you approach while they have something in their mouth
Responds equally with toys, food, and found objects
Turns toward you after dropping, expecting the trade
variations: Drop it in water (practice in pool or tub)
Drop it with food in mouth (snacks found on the street)
Drop it during tug-of-war play
Drop it with fabric objects (socks, clothing)
Drop it at a distance (when the dog is far from you)
safetyNotes: Never put your fingers in the mouth of an unknown or tense dog holding an object
If the dog frequently swallows objects, consult the vet (possible pica)
Do not use this technique as an excuse to always give food when the dog has something — the response must generalize
With a toxic or life-threatening object, use the trade without hesitation and move the dog away from the area
drop.funFact: Dogs that learn "drop it" correctly tend to play more confidently and spontaneously release objects during play, because they've learned that doing so brings good things.
drop.nextLevel: Combine "drop it" with "fetch" for a completely smooth retrieve game. Also practice "leave it" (don't pick up an object from the floor) as an essential complement.
drop.proTip: Practice "drop it" with objects your dog is allowed to have (toys), not just forbidden items. If the trade only appears when something bad is happening, the dog will learn to hide with whatever they find.

shake.title: Wave Hello
shake.subtitle: The crowd-pleasing trick everyone loves — saying hi with both paws!
shake.objective: Teach the dog to offer both paws alternately in a waving motion, responding to the verbal cue “wave” or a hand gesture.
why: It's a showstopper trick that impresses family and friends
Builds confidence and deepens the bond between dog and owner
Develops body awareness — the dog learns to control each paw independently
Opens the door to more advanced tricks like high five
benefits: Your dog learns to channel excitement into a specific, controlled behaviour
Improves coordination and balance in young dogs
Reduces uncontrolled jumping by redirecting energy into a precise action
Creates positive interaction moments that reinforce overall obedience
where: 🏠 Indoors, in the living room or kitchen without distractions
🌿 In the garden once it's well mastered indoors
🔇 Always in a calm space at the beginning
materials: 🫖 Small, high-value treats (chicken, cheese, sausage)
🛟 Non-slip surface so the dog feels secure
🖐️ Your open hands as the visual cue
💛 Patience and enthusiasm for every success
beforeYouStart: Your dog should reliably know “shake” with at least one paw before starting
Choose a calm moment — not right after an exciting walk and not when overtired
Prepare at least 20 small treats per session
Work on a non-slip surface (rug or carpet)
Keep sessions to 7 minutes maximum to maintain motivation

methods.title: Alternating paws wave method
methods.description: First consolidate shake with each paw separately, then alternate paws and speed up the motion until it looks like a natural wave.
methods.bestFor: Dogs that already know shake with one or both paws

steps.title: Consolidate the right paw
steps.description: Extend your right hand open and cue “right” (or whatever cue you use). When the dog offers the right paw, mark with “yes!” and reward immediately.
steps.tip: If the dog only knows one paw, repeat 5 times until the response is fluent.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog offers the wrong paw, ignore it silently and cue again.

steps.title: Consolidate the left paw
steps.description: Extend your left hand and cue “left”. Mark and reward every time the correct paw is offered. Spend 2–3 sessions on each side separately.
steps.tip: Keep hands symmetrical — same height, same gesture for each side.

steps.title: Alternate the paws
steps.description: Once both sides respond reliably, start alternating: right hand → “right”, reward; left hand → “left”, reward. Gradually increase the pace.
steps.tip: Start alternating every 3–4 seconds. Then reduce to 1–2 seconds.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog gets confused, go back to working each paw separately for a couple more sessions.

steps.title: Introduce the “wave” cue
steps.description: Once the dog alternates well, start saying “wave” before moving your hands. The dog will associate the word with the alternating motion.
steps.tip: Use an upbeat, festive tone when saying “wave” — the excitement is contagious.

steps.title: Speed up — the real wave
steps.description: Move your hands faster and lighter, mimicking a human wave. The dog will follow the rhythm and the result will look like a genuine wave with its paws.
steps.tip: Celebrate enthusiastically when the motion looks smooth and natural.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog loses rhythm, slow down again and build speed gradually.

commonErrors.error: Jumping to alternating before each paw is solid individually
commonErrors.cause: Rushing toward the final result
commonErrors.fix: Spend at least 3 sessions on each paw separately before combining them.

commonErrors.error: Using the same hand gesture for both paws
commonErrors.cause: Not visually distinguishing left from right
commonErrors.fix: Extend the hand on the same side as the paw you want. The visual signal is key.

commonErrors.error: Rewarding too late, after the paw has already come down
commonErrors.cause: Slow reflexes or treats not ready
commonErrors.fix: Hold treats in your free hand. Mark and reward at the moment of contact.

commonErrors.error: Sessions that are too long and bore the dog
commonErrors.cause: Trying to teach everything in one long session
commonErrors.fix: 7 minutes maximum. Always end on an easy success so the dog wants more.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog always offers the same paw
troubleshooting.solution: Work exclusively on the forgotten paw for 2–3 sessions. Only reward that paw until it balances out.

troubleshooting.problem: The dog lies down when I try to get the second paw
troubleshooting.solution: It's losing balance. Work on a firmer surface and ask for each paw with the dog well-planted on the other three.

troubleshooting.problem: The motion doesn't look like a wave — it's too slow
troubleshooting.solution: Use a smaller treat so the dog is more alert and active. Speed up your own hand and the dog will follow.

troubleshooting.problem: The dog gets overexcited and starts jumping
troubleshooting.solution: Stop the session, cue a “sit” to calm down, and restart. Lower your voice tone and reduce reward frequency.

progressMilestones.goal: Offers each paw separately in a fluid way in response to the correct hand
Alternates both paws when you switch hands, with small pauses between each
Responds to “wave” and alternates paws with increasing rhythm
Performs the wave smoothly in front of any familiar person

successSigns: Offers both paws alternately without confusion
Responds to “wave” before even seeing the hand gesture
The motion is fluid and has a natural wave rhythm
Does it in front of other people besides the owner
variations: Wave with only the right paw (classic shake)
Wave to different people (family members, friends)
Wave in rhythm to music
Wave from sitting and from standing position
Chain wave + bow for a complete performance
safetyNotes: Do not practice if the dog has any paw or joint injury
Large breed dogs: monitor they are not putting excessive weight on a single paw
If the dog shows resistance or limps, stop and consult a vet
Puppies under 6 months: sessions of 5 minutes maximum to protect developing joints
shake.funFact: Dogs naturally offer a paw as a social appeasement signal. When your dog gives you its paw, it's essentially saying: “I like you, I trust you.”
shake.nextLevel: Once the wave is mastered, try teaching high five and then chain them: wave → high five → bow. A complete three-trick performance!
shake.proTip: Use the highest-value treats for this trick because it requires more coordination. Your dog needs to feel it's really worth the effort.

spin.title: Spin (360°)
spin.subtitle: The most crowd-pleasing trick — a full circle on the spot!
