spin.objective: Teach the dog to spin a full 360° circle on cue, responding to the verbal cue “spin” or a circular hand gesture.
why: It's one of the most fun and eye-catching tricks to show in public
Improves body awareness and balance
Can be taught in both directions for twice the repertoire
Requires almost no space and zero special equipment
benefits: Mentally stimulates the dog and combats boredom
Improves flexibility and motor coordination
Can be used as a warm-up exercise before other activities
Makes the dog more attentive and motivated during training sessions
where: 🏠 Indoors, in any room with enough space for the dog to turn around
🌿 In the garden or park once mastered indoors
🔇 Always distraction-free at the start
materials: 🫖 Small high-value treats (chicken, cheese)
🖐️ One hand to guide the circular motion
🛟 Flat surface with no obstacles around
💛 Enthusiasm and vocal celebration
beforeYouStart: Your dog does not need any previous commands — this is a relatively easy starting trick
Make sure there's at least 1 metre of clear space around the dog
Prepare 20 small treats per session
Decide from the start whether you'll teach right or left first
Keep sessions to 5–7 minutes maximum

methods.title: Circular lure method
methods.description: Guide the dog with the treat describing a slow horizontal circle around its body. When it completes the turn, mark and reward. Then gradually fade the lure until only the gesture or voice is needed.
methods.bestFor: Any dog from 4 months, especially food-motivated ones

steps.title: Treat at the nose
steps.description: With the dog standing in front of you, place the treat right at its nose to get attention. The dog should follow the treat with its head.
steps.tip: If the dog jumps for the treat, wait until calm before starting.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog shows no interest in the treat, try a higher-value one (chicken, sausage).

steps.title: Start the circular arc
steps.description: Move the treat slowly to one side (for example, to the dog's right) keeping it at nose height. The dog will turn its head following the lure.
steps.tip: The movement must be slow and continuous. If too fast the dog will lose track.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog sits, restart from standing with the treat a little higher.

steps.title: Complete the circle
steps.description: Continue the circular movement around the dog's body, guiding the lure along the back, then the other flank, until the dog has completed the full 360° and is facing you again.
steps.tip: Keep the treat at nose height the whole time — never higher or lower.

steps.title: Name the trick
steps.description: When the dog completes the full circle, say “spin” in a happy tone and deliver the treat instantly.
steps.tip: Don't say “spin” before it tries — wait for the completed movement, then name it.

steps.title: Fade the lure
steps.description: After 5–6 sessions, start making the circular gesture without a treat in hand. When the dog completes the spin, reward from your pocket. Eventually use only a finger gesture or the voice.
steps.tip: Fade the lure gradually: first use a closed fist (no visible treat), then just the gesture.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog stops spinning without the lure, go back two steps and fade more slowly.

commonErrors.error: Moving the lure too fast
commonErrors.cause: Excitement about seeing the final result
commonErrors.fix: The lure must move at the dog's pace. If it loses track, restart more slowly.

commonErrors.error: Saying “spin” before the dog starts moving
commonErrors.cause: Wanting the cue to come before the behaviour
commonErrors.fix: Get the full spin with the lure first. Add the word only when the dog does it consistently.

commonErrors.error: Rewarding halfway through instead of at the end
commonErrors.cause: Celebrating too soon
commonErrors.fix: Hold the treat until the dog has completed the full circle and is facing you again.

commonErrors.error: Teaching both directions at the same time
commonErrors.cause: Wanting to progress faster
commonErrors.fix: Master one direction (e.g. right) over 3–4 sessions before introducing the other.

troubleshooting.problem: The dog only turns halfway and stops
troubleshooting.solution: Reward the half-spin at first (shaping) and extend the arc gradually session by session until reaching 360°.

troubleshooting.problem: The dog sits during the spin
troubleshooting.solution: The lure is too high. Keep the treat at nose height throughout the entire arc.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog refuses to turn in one direction
troubleshooting.solution: Normal — dogs have a preferred side. Work the difficult side in separate sessions.

troubleshooting.problem: Can spin but only with the lure in hand
troubleshooting.solution: Start using a closed fist (no visible treat) and reward from your pocket. Reduce the gesture size each week.

progressMilestones.goal: The dog follows the lure and completes at least half a turn
Completes the full 360° spin following the lure in 70% of attempts
Responds to “spin” with a reduced lure (closed fist)
Full spin with just the voice or a small circular finger gesture

successSigns: Completes the full 360° turn smoothly without pausing
Responds to “spin” before seeing the hand gesture
Can spin both right and left under different cues
Does it in different rooms and with people present
variations: Spin right on one cue, left on a different cue
Two spins in a row on a single command
Spin while walking alongside you
Spin at a distance (without being right in front of it)
Chain spin + bow for a complete crowd-pleasing finish
safetyNotes: Do not practice on slippery surfaces — the spin involves pivoting on the back legs
Dogs with hip or knee issues: consult a vet before teaching this trick
If the dog shows dizziness (odd head movements), start with half-turns
Puppies under 5 months: gentle turns and very short sessions to protect joints
spin.funFact: When a dog turns in circles before lying down, it's following an ancient instinct to flatten the grass and check for dangers. Your dog already spins naturally!
spin.nextLevel: Teach the spin in the opposite direction with a different word. Then combine: “spin right — spin left” in sequence. It looks like a choreographed dance!
spin.proTip: The secret is the lure rhythm: not too slow (loses interest) and not too fast (loses track). Move your hand at the pace of a slow waltz and your dog will spin perfectly.

high_five.title: High Five
high_five.subtitle: The coolest greeting between dog and owner — paw meets palm!
high_five.objective: Teach the dog to raise a paw vertically and touch the owner's open palm, responding to the verbal cue “high five” or a vertical open palm.
why: It's one of the most photogenic and fun tricks to share
Requires the dog to differentiate between “shake” (horizontal) and “high five” (vertical)
Builds coordination and awareness of paw position
Creates close, positive interaction with the owner and with new people
benefits: Improves focus and attention because the dog must watch the palm
Creates a shared celebration ritual — perfect for reinforcing good behaviour
It's a stepping stone to more complex tricks like clapping or targeting objects
Children love it and it makes socialisation with new people more positive
where: 🏠 Indoors, in the living room or kitchen
🌿 In the garden or park once it's well mastered
🔇 Without distractions at first — the trick requires precision
materials: 🫖 High-value treats (cooked chicken, cheese, sausage)
🖐️ Your open palm as the visual cue
🛟 Non-slip surface for better stability
💛 An enthusiastic vocal celebration for every success
beforeYouStart: Your dog should know “shake” reliably before starting
Make sure the surface is non-slip so the dog feels secure raising a paw
Prepare 20 small treats per session
Start with the dog's dominant paw (usually the left)
Keep sessions to 5–7 minutes maximum

methods.title: Progressive paw elevation method
methods.description: Start from shake at the normal low position and raise your palm gradually session by session until it is fully vertical. The dog learns that it must lift its paw higher each time to make contact.
methods.bestFor: Dogs that already know shake

steps.title: Shake at normal height
steps.description: Cue “shake” with your palm facing up at the usual height. Mark and reward when it touches your hand.
steps.tip: This is the starting point. Do 5 repetitions to warm up.
steps.troubleshooting: If shake isn't reliable, spend 2–3 sessions consolidating it first.

steps.title: Raise the palm gradually
steps.description: Each session, raise your palm a few centimetres. The dog will have to lift its paw higher to touch it. Keep the palm horizontal at first.
steps.tip: Don't raise more than 3–5 cm per session. Gradual progression is the key.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog can't reach the hand, lower a little and work that height more before going higher.

steps.title: Rotate palm to vertical
steps.description: Once the dog brings its paw up to chest height, start rotating your palm to a vertical position (as if offering a handshake to someone). The dog will touch the palm head-on.
steps.tip: The visual cue of a vertical palm will become the definitive signal for “high five”.

steps.title: Introduce the “high five” cue
steps.description: When the dog consistently touches your vertical palm, add “high five” just before extending your hand. Mark the contact and reward enthusiastically.
steps.tip: Use a festive, celebratory tone — this trick deserves a party.
steps.troubleshooting: If it confuses “high five” with “shake”, work them in different contexts and use clearly different gestures.

steps.title: Differentiate between shake and high five
steps.description: Practice alternating both signals so the dog distinguishes them: palm horizontal facing down = “shake”; palm vertical facing the dog = “high five”. Reward the correct response with higher value.
steps.tip: Signal differentiation is the most advanced level. Don't rush it.

commonErrors.error: Raising the hand too fast before the dog consolidates each height
commonErrors.cause: Impatience to reach the full high five
commonErrors.fix: Spend at least 2 sessions at each height before going higher. Quality matters more than speed.

commonErrors.error: Accepting the dog scratching the hand instead of touching with a flat paw
commonErrors.cause: Not marking precisely what type of contact is wanted
commonErrors.fix: Only mark clean flat-paw contact. Ignore scratches without rewarding them.

commonErrors.error: Not differentiating the visual signals between shake and high five
commonErrors.cause: Using the same gesture for both tricks
commonErrors.fix: Horizontal palm for “shake”, vertical palm for “high five”. Train this difference actively.

commonErrors.error: Rewarding with low energy — the trick feels boring
commonErrors.cause: Sparse or monotone celebration
commonErrors.fix: High five deserves euphoria! Raise your voice, smile big, and add a “great job!” with conviction.

troubleshooting.problem: The dog touches the hand with its nose instead of its paw
troubleshooting.solution: Withdraw your hand when the nose approaches and offer it again. Only mark paw contact.

troubleshooting.problem: The dog loses balance raising the paw very high
troubleshooting.solution: Work on a non-slip surface and don't raise the hand so high yet. Balance will improve with practice.

troubleshooting.problem: Can't differentiate between “shake” and “high five”
troubleshooting.solution: Exaggerate the gesture difference and work each signal in separate sessions for a week before mixing them.

troubleshooting.problem: Does it well at home but not with other people
troubleshooting.solution: Start by showing the trick to family members at home. Then with friends. Generalisation takes time.

progressMilestones.goal: Raises the paw at least to elbow height in response to the palm
Touches the vertical palm at chest height consistently
Responds to “high five” at full high five height
Clearly differentiates between “shake” and “high five” and does it with other people

successSigns: Raises paw to the vertical palm without hesitation
Responds to “high five” before even seeing the palm
Does it with other people besides the owner
Clearly distinguishes between “shake” and “high five”
variations: High five with left paw and right paw
High five at different heights (low, mid, high)
High five from a distance (50 cm away)
Chain high five + bow for a complete routine
High ten: both paws simultaneously against both palms
safetyNotes: Never force the paw upward with your hand — let the dog raise it on its own
Dogs with shoulder or elbow issues: consult a vet before practicing
If the dog shows discomfort raising the paw, stop the session and check for limping
Puppies under 6 months: limit height to protect developing joints
high_five.funFact: Dogs that learn “high five” often start offering it spontaneously when they want attention — your dog may become addicted to giving you high fives out of nowhere.
high_five.nextLevel: Teach the high ten (both paws at once). Then chain: wave → high five → bow. You have a complete three-trick performance!
high_five.proTip: When the dog nails a perfect high five, celebrate with the biggest reaction you can manage. Dogs learn fastest when the emotional reward is huge.

roll_over.title: Roll Over
roll_over.subtitle: The most impressive trick — a complete flip from the ground up!
roll_over.objective: Teach the dog to roll a full 360° from the down position, passing through the side and returning to the down position, responding to the cue “roll over”.
why: It's the most spectacular trick in the basic repertoire — always surprises and delights
Requires the dog to fully trust its owner to expose itself in a vulnerable position
Improves flexibility, body awareness, and coordination
Demonstrates the highest level of communication and understanding between dog and owner
benefits: Builds the bond and trust in an extraordinary way
Excellent physical exercise for the flexibility of the spine and flanks
Once mastered, the dog performs it smoothly and elegantly
The starting point for more complex performance tricks
where: 🏠 Exclusively indoors on a very soft surface at first
🛏️ Thick rug, folded blanket, or yoga mat — essential
⛔ Never on hard, cold, or slippery floors — the dog must feel comfortable in the side-lying position
materials: 🫖 Maximum-value treats (cooked chicken, strong cheese, sausage)
🛟 Yoga mat, thick rug, or folded blanket
🖐️ Your hand to guide the lure
💛 Extra patience — this trick is learned phase by phase, not all at once
beforeYouStart: Your dog must master “down” very reliably — it is the mandatory starting point
Use the softest, most comfortable surface you have: blanket, mat, or thick rug
Bring the highest-value treats — this trick is demanding and deserves the best reward
Work in phases: don't attempt the full roll on the first day
Maximum 5-minute sessions — the trick requires significant physical and mental effort

methods.title: Over-the-shoulder lure method
methods.description: From the down position, guide the lure toward the dog's shoulder so it turns its head, then the body follows through to complete the roll. Work phase by phase: head turn → shoulder on floor → full roll.
methods.bestFor: Dogs that master the down and have good trust with their owner

steps.title: Ask for down on the mat
steps.description: Cue “down” on the soft surface. The dog should be completely relaxed, with elbows and chest on the floor.
steps.tip: Wait until it is genuinely comfortable before continuing. A tense dog will not roll well.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog gets up when it sees the treat, first work on maintaining the down with distractions.

steps.title: Guide the head toward the shoulder — Phase 1
steps.description: With the treat at its nose, move it slowly toward the shoulder on the side you want it to roll. The dog will turn its head following the lure. Mark and reward the head turn only.
steps.tip: Reward this phase generously for 3–4 sessions. Don't move on until it happens naturally.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog gets up instead of turning its head, restart the down and go slower.

steps.title: Shoulder touches the floor — Phase 2
steps.description: Continue guiding the treat past the shoulder, toward the floor on the opposite side. The body will follow the head and the shoulder will touch the floor. The dog is now in the full side-lying position. Mark and reward.
steps.tip: This is the hardest phase because the dog exposes itself in a vulnerable position. Use the highest-value treat.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog resists going onto its side, slow the lure down and reward every small bit of progress.

steps.title: Body completes the roll — Phase 3
steps.description: With the dog on its side, continue the arc of the lure over the back toward the other side. The dog will roll through, completing 360° and landing back in the normal down position. Mark and celebrate enthusiastically.
steps.tip: When the dog completes the full roll for the first time, celebrate as if it's the best thing you've ever seen.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog only gets halfway, reward there and extend a little more each session.

steps.title: Name the trick and fade the lure
steps.description: When the full roll is consistent, say “roll over” just before starting the lure. Gradually reduce the gesture until the dog rolls with just the voice or a small wrist rotation.
steps.tip: Fade the lure very gradually: visible treat → closed fist → gesture only → voice only.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog stops rolling when you reduce the lure, go back to the full lure and fade more slowly.

commonErrors.error: Attempting the full roll from the very first session
commonErrors.cause: Wanting to see the final result too soon
commonErrors.fix: Work in phases. Spend at least 3–4 sessions on each phase before moving on.

commonErrors.error: Moving the lure too fast and losing the dog halfway
commonErrors.cause: Lure moving faster than the dog can follow
commonErrors.fix: The lure must move at the dog's pace. If the dog gets up, you're going too fast.

commonErrors.error: Practicing on a hard or cold floor
commonErrors.cause: Not preparing the environment properly
commonErrors.fix: A soft surface is non-negotiable. The dog needs to feel comfortable in the side-lying position.

commonErrors.error: Forcing the dog onto its side with your hand
commonErrors.cause: Frustration when the lure is not working
commonErrors.fix: Never use physical force. If the lure isn't working, use a higher-value treat or return to the previous phase.

troubleshooting.problem: The dog turns its head but not its body
troubleshooting.solution: You're in Phase 1 — this is normal. Keep rewarding only the head turn until it's automatic. The body will follow naturally after.

troubleshooting.problem: The dog gets up every time the lure approaches the shoulder
troubleshooting.solution: Work on maintaining the down with more distractions first. The dog needs more confidence in holding the position.

troubleshooting.problem: The dog makes it to the side but won't complete the roll
troubleshooting.solution: Reward the side position generously for several sessions. Then guide the lure 10° further each time.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog only rolls in one direction
troubleshooting.solution: This is normal and valid. Many dogs prefer one side. Consolidate that side well before attempting the other direction.

progressMilestones.goal: Turns its head toward the shoulder following the lure from the down position
Shoulder touches the floor and the dog reaches the full side-lying position
Completes the full 360° roll following the lure
Responds to “roll over” with a reduced lure or voice only

successSigns: Completes the full 360° roll smoothly without pausing in the side position
Ends in the down position and looks at the owner waiting for the reward
Responds to the verbal cue without needing the full lure
Does it on different soft surfaces (rug, blanket, mat)
variations: Roll over to the other direction
Two rolls in a row on a single cue
Slow, controlled roll (harder than a fast one)
Chain down → roll over → sit for a smooth sequence
safetyNotes: Never practice with dogs with back, hip, or dysplasia issues without consulting a vet
Never force the dog onto its side — if it doesn't do it voluntarily, it's not ready
Dogs over 8 years: consult a vet before teaching this trick
If the dog shows stiffness, discomfort, or avoids the side-lying position, stop and observe for 48 hours
roll_over.funFact: Dogs show their belly as the ultimate signal of trust and appeasement. When your dog rolls over for you, it's saying it feels completely safe in your presence.
roll_over.nextLevel: Chain: down → roll over → sit → high five. Four tricks in a row that will leave everyone speechless!
roll_over.proTip: Always work in the direction the dog naturally chooses at first. Once that side is mastered, the opposite side will come much more easily.

bow.title: Take a Bow
bow.subtitle: The most elegant trick — like an actor bowing to the audience
bow.objective: Teach the dog to lower its chest toward the floor while keeping its rear end up (the play bow position), responding to the cue “bow” or “take a bow”.
why: The bow is a posture dogs perform completely naturally when inviting play
It's the most visually elegant trick — it looks like a performer bowing to an audience
Reinforces body awareness by dissociating the movement of the front from the rear
It's the perfect finishing move to close any sequence of tricks
benefits: Excellent stretch for the back and shoulders — it works like canine yoga
Allows the dog to communicate its desire to play in a natural way
Easy to learn because it captures an instinctive behaviour
Generates very positive reactions from everyone who sees it
where: 🏠 Indoors, in any room with enough space
🌿 In the garden or outdoors once mastered indoors
🔇 Without distractions at first so the dog can focus
materials: 🫖 Small high-value treats
🖐️ Your hand as the lure (treat between fingers)
🛟 Flat, comfortable surface
💛 Patience and watchful eyes to capture the natural behaviour
beforeYouStart: Watch your dog during the day — it almost certainly already does the bow naturally when stretching or inviting play
The trick can be taught by capturing (catching the natural behaviour) or by luring
Keep treats handy at all times during the day to capture the moment
Maximum 5-minute sessions — short and frequent
Your dog needs no prior tricks to learn this one

methods.title: Combined capture and lure method
methods.description: First try capturing the natural bows the dog already does. If they happen frequently, mark and reward them until you can name the behaviour. If the dog doesn't bow much spontaneously, use the lure by guiding the treat between its front paws toward the floor while gently blocking the hip with your forearm.
methods.bestFor: Any dog — adapt the method depending on whether it bows naturally often or rarely

steps.title: Watch for natural bows
steps.description: For 2–3 days, notice when your dog bows naturally (on waking, when inviting play). When it happens, say “yes!” and hurry to give a treat.
steps.tip: Keep treats in your pocket or near where it usually stretches in the morning.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog hardly ever bows spontaneously, go straight to the lure method.

steps.title: Capture and mark the behaviour
steps.description: Each time you catch a natural bow, mark with “yes!” at the exact moment the chest is low and the rear is up, and reward immediately.
steps.tip: Timing precision is crucial: mark when the chest is at its lowest, not as it's already rising.

steps.title: Lure between the front legs (if capture doesn't work)
steps.description: With the dog standing, guide the lure from its nose down to the floor between its front legs. Use your free forearm to gently block the hip so it doesn't lie down. The dog will lower its chest following the treat.
steps.tip: The forearm under the belly acts as a gentle guide — never as a forced restraint.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog lies down completely, withdraw the lure and try again with less downward movement.

steps.title: Name the trick
steps.description: When the dog performs the correct posture (chest low, rear high) consistently, add the word “bow” or “take a bow” just before starting the lure.
steps.tip: Use a soft, elegant tone — the bow is a trick with class.

steps.title: Fade the lure and generalise
steps.description: Gradually reduce the lure movement: first with a treat in hand, then with an empty gesture, finally with just the word. Practice in different places and with different people present.
steps.tip: The bow posture is easy to hold for 2–3 seconds. Reward while maintained to extend duration.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog goes back to lying down, return to the lure with the supporting forearm for more sessions.

commonErrors.error: Dropping the lure so fast that the dog lies down instead of bowing
commonErrors.cause: Too direct a movement toward the floor
commonErrors.fix: Lower the lure very slowly between the front legs. Block the hip gently with your forearm if needed.

commonErrors.error: Not marking the exact moment of the bow
commonErrors.cause: Imprecise reward timing
commonErrors.fix: Mark when the chest is at its lowest and the rear is up. If you mark too late, you're reinforcing the standing back up.

commonErrors.error: Missing the natural bows during the day by not having treats ready
commonErrors.cause: Not having treats nearby
commonErrors.fix: Carry treats in your pocket during the first couple of weeks to capture spontaneous bows.

commonErrors.error: Confusing the bow with the down
commonErrors.cause: The lure moves too far forward instead of staying between the front legs
commonErrors.fix: The lure goes to the floor between the front legs, not forward. This forces the chest down without lowering the rear.

troubleshooting.problem: The dog always lies down completely instead of bowing
troubleshooting.solution: Use your forearm under its belly as a gentle guide. You can also practice with the dog facing a low sofa so the rear legs stay slightly elevated.

troubleshooting.problem: The bow lasts only an instant and the dog stands up immediately
troubleshooting.solution: Reward while holding the posture (not just when arriving at it). Start rewarding at 0.5 seconds and gradually build to 1, 2, 3 seconds.

troubleshooting.problem: The dog bows naturally when it wants to play but not when asked
troubleshooting.solution: Use those moments to name it. Then use the lure to provoke it in a controlled way outside the play context.

troubleshooting.problem: Can't keep the rear up while lowering the chest
troubleshooting.solution: The forearm under the belly is the most effective solution. Or practice on a low step with the rear legs elevated.

progressMilestones.goal: The dog bows naturally at least 3 times a day and you mark and reward it
Lowers its chest following the lure while keeping the rear up
Responds to “bow” with a reduced lure
Holds the posture for 3–5 seconds and performs it with voice only or a small gesture

successSigns: Lowers chest to the floor while clearly keeping the rear up
Holds the posture for at least 2 seconds before the reward
Responds to “bow” without needing the full lure
Does it in different places and in front of different people
variations: Slow, sustained bow (more theatrical and elegant)
Bow with a head dip (add a second lure to lower the head too)
Bow facing a mirror so the dog sees its own posture
Chain bow at the start and end of a tricks sequence
Bow + direct camera eye contact (perfect for photos)
safetyNotes: Dogs with spinal or shoulder issues: consult a vet before practicing
If the dog shows stiffness or discomfort lowering the chest, stop the session
Do not use the forearm as a restriction — only as a passive, gentle guide
Puppies under 5 months: very short sessions and do not force the posture
bow.funFact: The play bow is one of the most universal signals in canine body language. Every dog in the world uses it to say “shall we play?” — you're simply putting a name to it.
bow.nextLevel: Chain: sit → high five → bow. A complete three-step greeting that any dog can learn in 3 weeks.
bow.proTip: If your dog bows naturally every morning when it wakes up, that's the perfect moment to capture and name it. Keep treats on your bedside table — seriously!

leave_it.title: Leave It
leave_it.subtitle: The most important safety command your dog can learn
leave_it.objective: Teach your dog to ignore any object on the ground or in your hand when they hear the cue 'leave it', protecting them from ingesting dangerous items.
why: Protects your dog from eating dangerous food, garbage or toxins on the street
Controls impulses around tempting objects without needing to yank the leash
Builds trust between dog and owner through self-control
Lays the foundation for better exploration behavior in new environments
benefits: Your dog ignores food dropped on the floor before you can pick it up
Prevents resource conflicts with other dogs
Reduces the risk of accidental poisoning during walks
Develops self-control as a transferable skill for other situations
where: 🏠 Start at home in a distraction-free room
🌿 Progress to the garden or patio once they've mastered it indoors
🛣️ Finally practice on the street with real-life distractions
materials: 🫖 Two types of treats: low-value (kibble) and high-value (chicken, cheese)
✋ Your hands as the treat 'hiding spot'
🦮 Long leash (optional for outdoor practice)
💛 Patience and a calm demeanor
beforeYouStart: Have two types of treats ready: one to use as the 'temptation' and a better one to reward with
Make sure your dog has a minimum level of attention toward you
Practice off-leash at home before moving outdoors
Keep sessions to a maximum of 5 minutes to avoid overwhelming your dog
Don't practice if your dog is very hungry or overly excited

methods.title: Closed fist method (recommended to start)
methods.description: You hide a treat in your closed hand, the dog tries to get it, and when they back off you reward them with a different and better treat. Teaches that ignoring = earning something better.
methods.bestFor: Puppies and dogs with no prior experience with the command

steps.title: Make the fist
steps.description: Place a low-value treat in your hand and close it into a fist. Offer the closed fist to the dog at nose level.
steps.tip: Use a low-value treat here (regular kibble); the good treat goes in your other hand or pocket.
steps.troubleshooting: If your dog barks or paws intensely, hold steady. Don't pull your hand away or scold them.

steps.title: Observe and wait
steps.description: Your dog will sniff, lick and push at your fist trying to get the treat. Don't open your hand. Wait in silence.
steps.tip: Patience is key. The first time it may take anywhere from 10 seconds to 2 minutes.
steps.troubleshooting: If they lose interest and walk away, try a more enticing smell but still only reward when they back off.

steps.title: Capture the withdrawal
steps.description: The moment your dog pulls their nose away from your fist (even by a centimetre), say 'leave it' and immediately reward with the good treat from your other hand.
steps.tip: Timing is critical: the reward must arrive within 2 seconds of them backing away.

steps.title: Repeat and increase difficulty
steps.description: Repeat 5–8 times per session. Once they do it fluidly, begin placing an object on the floor covered by your foot.
steps.tip: Increase difficulty gradually: fist → floor covered → floor visible → street.

steps.title: Generalize the command
steps.description: Once they master it with your fist, practice with objects on the floor, dropped food, and then outdoors with real distractions.
steps.tip: In every new environment, go back to the easiest level before increasing difficulty.

methods.title: Ground progression method
methods.description: You start with the treat covered by your foot and gradually uncover it as the dog learns to resist the temptation. Ideal for consolidating the command.
methods.bestFor: Dogs that already understand the basic concept from the fist method or have higher impulse

steps.title: Treat under the foot
steps.description: Place a treat on the floor and cover it completely with the tip of your foot. Allow your dog to sniff around your foot.
steps.tip: Your foot must fully cover the treat so they can't steal it.
steps.troubleshooting: If they scratch the floor intensely, don't react. Wait calmly until they back away.

steps.title: Say 'leave it' and wait
steps.description: When your dog backs away even slightly from your foot, say 'leave it' calmly and reward with a treat from your hand (not the one on the floor).
steps.tip: Never reward with the floor treat: the dog must learn that 'leave it' means 'that treat isn't yours, but you earn a better one'.

steps.title: Gradually uncover
steps.description: Once the dog waits without trying to grab the floor treat, move your foot very slightly to reveal a small part of the treat. Repeat the command.
steps.tip: If they lunge, cover it again with your foot. No scolding — just reset.

steps.title: Treat fully visible
steps.description: The final goal is for your dog to see the treat on the floor and ignore it when they hear 'leave it', looking at you instead in anticipation of the reward.
steps.tip: This step may require 3–5 additional sessions. Don't rush.

commonErrors.error: Repeating 'leave it' multiple times in a row
commonErrors.cause: Owner frustration when the dog doesn't respond on the first try
commonErrors.fix: Say the command ONCE and wait in silence. Repeating it teaches your dog to ignore it.

commonErrors.error: Rewarding with the object they were told to leave
commonErrors.cause: Using whatever is most convenient to reward with
commonErrors.fix: Always reward with a DIFFERENT and higher-value treat. The forbidden object must never become the reward.

commonErrors.error: Using the command in real dangerous situations without prior training
commonErrors.cause: Assuming the dog knows it without systematic practice
commonErrors.fix: Practice at home weeks before needing it on the street. In real emergencies, physically remove your dog.

commonErrors.error: Scolding the dog when they grab the object
commonErrors.cause: Impulsive reaction of frustration
commonErrors.fix: Never punish. If they grabbed it, the training needs more foundational steps. Go back to an earlier level.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog grabs the treat before I can say 'leave it'
troubleshooting.solution: The object is too accessible. Go back to the closed fist and make sure you control access before advancing.

troubleshooting.problem: They do 'leave it' at home but it doesn't work on the street
troubleshooting.solution: Normal: the street has more stimuli. Restart training outdoors from the easiest step, with fewer distractions first.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog gets frustrated and barks when I say 'leave it'
troubleshooting.solution: Impulse is high. Practice in shorter sessions (2–3 minutes) with higher-value rewards and reduce the appeal of the forbidden object.

troubleshooting.problem: Works fine with food but not with objects (socks, toys)
troubleshooting.solution: These are different categories for your dog. Train specifically with each type of object, starting with those of lower value to them.

progressMilestones.goal: Dog pulls nose away from the closed fist at least once per session
Ignores the fist in 7 out of 10 attempts and starts looking at you for the good treat
Ignores a visible treat on the floor covered by your foot when they hear 'leave it'
Ignores objects on the floor without the foot covering them, at home and in the garden

successSigns: Backs away from the object and looks at you spontaneously when they hear 'leave it'
Works with different types of objects (food, toys, garbage)
Performs in outdoor settings with moderate distractions
Maintains distance from the object for 5 or more seconds
variations: Leave it with food in your open palm (advanced level)
Leave it with another dog as the distractor
Leave it with an object suddenly tossed to the floor
Leave it while walking (without stopping)
Leave it with a waiting period before receiving the alternative reward
safetyNotes: In real danger situations (toxin, glass) don't rely on the command: act directly
Never use physical or verbal punishment when your dog fails: just reset the exercise
Make sure reward treats are not toxic to dogs (no xylitol, grapes, onion)
If your dog shows resource guarding or growling when you approach the object, consult a certified behaviorist before continuing
leave_it.funFact: Dogs that learn 'leave it' in their first weeks of life have up to 40% fewer vet visits for ingesting foreign objects.
leave_it.nextLevel: Practice 'leave it' while moving during walks. Then introduce it with other dogs or animals as the distractor.
leave_it.proTip: The secret of 'leave it' is that the dog learns ignoring something always produces something better. Never skimp on the quality of the reward treat — it must be clearly superior to the forbidden object.

fetch.title: Fetch
fetch.subtitle: Play, exercise and obedience all in one command
fetch.location: Garden, park or long hallway at home
fetch.objective: Teach your dog to chase a thrown object, pick it up, bring it back to the owner, and release it — completing the full retrieve cycle.
why: One of the most efficient ways to give a dog physical and mental exercise
Reinforces the bond between owner and dog through play
Teaches the concept of voluntary exchange, the foundation of many other behaviours
Provides an energy-release channel for high-drive dogs
benefits: Your dog is physically and mentally tired in 15 minutes, reducing destructive behaviours
Learns to release objects voluntarily, reducing resource guarding
Anticipation of the throw improves attention and focus
Can be practised in small spaces with soft objects
where: 🏡 Fenced garden or yard to start
🌳 Park with enclosed or grassy area
🏠 Long home hallway with a soft ball (beginning)
materials: 🎾 Two identical or similar toys or balls
🫖 High-value treats (optional, for early sessions)
🦮 Long line of 5–10 m (for dogs that don't return)
💛 Enthusiasm and an animated voice
beforeYouStart: Check if your dog has a chase instinct: toss a ball and see if they pursue it
Choose an enclosed space without escape risk for the first sessions
Have two toys ready: this is key for the two-toy method
Sessions no longer than 10–15 minutes to avoid fatigue
If the dog has never played, start with the object on the floor before throwing

methods.title: Two-toy method (recommended)
methods.description: You use two identical toys alternating them: when the dog brings the first one back, you excitedly show the second one so they drop it. Builds the return habit without teaching 'drop it' separately.
methods.bestFor: Dogs with a chase instinct that don't drop or don't come back

steps.title: Two toys in hand
steps.description: Start with both toys in your hands, behind your back or hidden. Show only one to your dog to generate interest.
steps.tip: The toys must be appealing. Play a little with the first one before throwing to increase its value.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog shows no interest, wiggle the toy near them before throwing.

steps.title: First throw
steps.description: Throw toy #1 enthusiastically. Wait for your dog to chase and grab it.
steps.tip: Throw only a few metres at first. Distance increases with practice.
steps.troubleshooting: If they don't chase it, make the toy more interesting: move it on the floor like prey before throwing.

steps.title: Show toy #2
steps.description: When the dog has toy #1 in their mouth and starts coming back (even partially), pull out toy #2 with great excitement: wiggle it, make it interesting.
steps.tip: Your attitude is key. The dog must want toy #2 more than the one in their mouth.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog stays put with the toy, turn your back: dogs want what we ignore.

steps.title: Exchange and drop
steps.description: When the dog comes to you seeking toy #2, they'll drop toy #1 voluntarily. At that moment, throw toy #2 as the reward.
steps.tip: Don't say 'drop it': the exchange makes it natural. Say 'yes' or 'good' when they drop it.

steps.title: Continuous cycle
steps.description: Pick up toy #1 and repeat the cycle. The dog learns: bring it back = the fun starts again.
steps.tip: End the session yourself while the dog still wants more. This keeps the drive for the next session.

methods.title: Shaping method (for dogs without retrieve instinct)
methods.description: You reinforce any progressive approach to the toy: looking → approaching → sniffing → touching → picking up → bringing one step closer. Ideal for dogs that show no natural interest in chasing.
methods.bestFor: Dogs without natural retrieve instinct, non-retriever breeds, or older dogs

steps.title: Look at the toy
steps.description: Place the toy on the floor. Every time the dog looks at it, say 'yes' and reward. Don't ask for more yet.
steps.tip: A clicker is very useful in this method to mark exactly the right behaviour.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog doesn't look at the toy, move it slightly to attract their attention.

steps.title: Approach the toy
steps.description: Now only reward if the dog moves toward the toy, not just looks at it. Raise the criteria slowly.
steps.tip: Each step must be small. If the dog gets frustrated, return to the previous step.

steps.title: Touch or pick up the toy
steps.description: Reward when the dog touches the toy with their nose or picks it up with their mouth, even briefly.
steps.tip: Any contact with the toy is a success at this stage. Don't demand perfection yet.

steps.title: Bring it one step toward you
steps.description: Reward only when the dog picks up the toy AND takes at least one step toward you. Gradually increase the required distance.
steps.tip: Step backward yourself to make it easier for the dog to approach. Your movement invites their movement.

steps.title: Full retrieve
steps.description: Once they consistently bring the toy to you, add the exchange (a food treat in return for the toy) to complete the cycle.
steps.tip: Replace the food treat with a toy throw once the dog understands the concept well.

commonErrors.error: Chasing the dog to recover the toy
commonErrors.cause: Frustration when the dog doesn't come back
commonErrors.fix: Never run after them: you turn it into a 'catch me if you can' game. Turn your back or run in the opposite direction.

commonErrors.error: Forcing the mouth open to take the toy
commonErrors.cause: Impatience to throw again
commonErrors.fix: Always use the exchange (second toy or treat). Forced opening can create resource guarding.

commonErrors.error: Sessions too long that exhaust the dog
commonErrors.cause: The dog shows initial enthusiasm and the owner doesn't stop in time
commonErrors.fix: Always stop before the dog gets tired. Short sessions maintain drive and enthusiasm.

commonErrors.error: Throwing the toy when the dog jumps or pushes
commonErrors.cause: Giving in to the dog's pressure
commonErrors.fix: Only throw when the dog is calm or in a sit position. This teaches self-control before play.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog chases the toy but won't pick it up
troubleshooting.solution: Try a softer, more appealing toy. You can also make the toy 'flee' from them by moving it to activate prey instinct.

troubleshooting.problem: They pick it up but don't come back
troubleshooting.solution: Use a long line to gently guide them toward you while showing great enthusiasm for toy #2. Never yank.

troubleshooting.problem: They come back but won't drop the toy
troubleshooting.solution: Two-toy method: the second toy always triggers dropping the first. If not, offer a very high-value food treat.

troubleshooting.problem: They lose interest after 2–3 throws
troubleshooting.solution: Sessions are too long or the toy isn't motivating enough. Try a different toy and shorter sessions (3–5 throws, then stop).

progressMilestones.goal: The dog chases the thrown toy and picks it up at least once
Returns to you with the toy in 50% of attempts
Completes the full cycle (chase, pick up, return, drop) consistently
Performs the full retrieve outdoors with moderate distractions

successSigns: Chases the toy immediately when thrown
Returns to you with the toy without being called
Drops the toy when they see the second one or hear 'drop it'
Maintains enthusiasm throughout the entire session
variations: Fetch by object name ('get the ball', 'get the rope')
Fetch in water (for dogs that enjoy swimming)
Fetch specific objects (find the keys, find the remote)
Fetch from progressively greater distances (5m → 20m → 50m)
Fetch with obstacles or between trees
safetyNotes: Never throw small objects that could be swallowed
Avoid throwing sticks: they can cause serious mouth and throat injuries
Limit intense play in dogs with hip dysplasia or joint problems
On hot days, very short sessions with water available: fetch is very demanding
fetch.funFact: Golden Retrievers and Labradors were genetically selected to retrieve prey without damaging it (soft mouth). That's why many learn fetch almost instinctively.
fetch.nextLevel: Teach the names of different objects so the dog can search for and bring the correct one. Or introduce water retrieval if your dog enjoys swimming.
fetch.proTip: Fetch breaks down almost always for two reasons: the dog won't drop or won't come back. Universal solution: always have a second toy and never, ever chase your dog.

wait.title: Wait
wait.subtitle: Brief pause with self-control in everyday situations
wait.objective: Teach your dog to pause momentarily on a verbal cue, applicable before crossing the street, before receiving their food bowl, or when crossing thresholds. Different from 'stay' — it's shorter and more contextual.
why: Prevents accidents at street crossings by stopping your dog from running ahead
Teaches self-control during high-excitement moments (feeding time, entering the park)
Establishes a safe door protocol to prevent escapes
A real safety skill with immediate application in daily life
benefits: Your dog stops before crossing any dangerous threshold
Learns to control excitement at feeding time
Reduces anxiety during transitions (indoors-outdoors, car-street)
Improves communication and trust between dog and owner
where: 🚪 Indoor and outdoor doorways and thresholds
🍽️ Your dog's feeding area
🛣️ Before crossing pedestrian crossings or streets
materials: 🍗 Dog's food bowl or high-value treats
🚪 Actual door or threshold to practise at
🦮 Leash (optional for street practice)
💛 Consistency and calm
beforeYouStart: Choose one specific situation to start with: the food bowl is ideal because it happens daily
Always follow the same protocol in that situation so the dog anticipates it
Make sure the dog is not in an extreme state of excitement when you start
Short sessions: 3–5 repetitions per context is enough
Have treats ready or the actual food bowl on hand

methods.title: Food bowl protocol
methods.description: You use feeding time as natural daily training. Bowl goes down → dog waits → bowl rises if they move → reward when patient. Simple, repeatable and with immediate impact.
methods.bestFor: All dogs, especially those that lunge at the bowl or push the owner at feeding time

steps.title: Dog in a sit
steps.description: Before preparing the bowl, ask your dog to sit. If they don't know 'sit' fluently, start with that course first.
steps.tip: The sit is not mandatory, but it helps: a sitting dog has more self-control than a standing one.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog won't sit, wait standing with the bowl in hand until they calm down, even for a moment.

steps.title: Say 'wait' and begin lowering the bowl
steps.description: With the bowl in your hands, say 'wait' calmly and begin slowly lowering the bowl toward the floor.
steps.tip: The verbal cue must come before the movement, not after. The dog should learn that 'wait' predicts food if they are patient.

steps.title: If they move, raise the bowl
steps.description: If the dog stands up, moves forward or touches the bowl before the release, immediately raise the bowl without saying anything. Return to the previous step.
steps.tip: No scolding: the rising bowl is enough information. No drama.
steps.troubleshooting: If they keep repeating the movement, lower the bowl only 5 cm and reward from there. Increase distance little by little.

steps.title: Bowl on the floor, dog waits
steps.description: When the bowl touches the floor and the dog waits without moving, pause 1–2 seconds, then say 'okay' or 'go' to give the release.
steps.tip: The release word is as important as 'wait'. Always use the same one.

steps.title: Gradually increase wait time
steps.description: Start with 1–2 seconds of waiting with the bowl on the floor. Gradually increase to 5, 10, 15 seconds before the release.
steps.tip: If they fail at any point, go back to a shorter time. Progress is not linear and that's normal.

commonErrors.error: Repeating 'wait' while the bowl is already on the floor
commonErrors.cause: Owner nervousness when seeing the dog approach the bowl
commonErrors.fix: Say 'wait' ONCE before lowering the bowl. If they move, raise the bowl without saying anything.

commonErrors.error: Giving the release before the dog is completely still
commonErrors.cause: Rushing or wanting to avoid conflict
commonErrors.fix: Wait until the dog is clearly motionless for at least 1 second before giving the release.

commonErrors.error: Confusing 'wait' with 'stay'
commonErrors.cause: Using both commands interchangeably
commonErrors.fix: 'Wait' is brief and contextual (seconds). 'Stay' means holding the position until a new signal. Use them in different contexts.

commonErrors.error: Not practising the doorway as a separate situation
commonErrors.cause: Assuming that learning with the bowl transfers automatically
commonErrors.fix: Practise 'wait' specifically at doors, gates and street crossings. Each context needs its own training.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog waits but stares at me with extreme anxiety
troubleshooting.solution: The wait is too long for their current level. Reduce the wait time to whatever they can do without stress (even 1 second) and increase very slowly.

troubleshooting.problem: They learn well with the bowl but still bolt through the door
troubleshooting.solution: Normal: these are different contexts. Practise the door protocol just like the bowl: if they advance, close the door. If they wait, open it and give the release.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog waits but slowly creeps toward the bowl
troubleshooting.solution: Creeping counts as movement. Raise the bowl. Only reward when they are completely still.

troubleshooting.problem: Only works when I have the bowl in my hand, not with treats on the floor
troubleshooting.solution: Train the bowl first until consolidated. Then practise with treats on the floor using the same progression: hand → covered floor → visible floor.

progressMilestones.goal: Dog waits at least 1–2 seconds with the bowl on the floor before the release
Waits 10 seconds with the bowl on the floor without moving
Applies 'wait' at the doorway as well
Waits consistently at street crossings and before getting out of the car

successSigns: Dog stops when they hear 'wait' before moving toward the bowl or door
Waits without moving their body even with the bowl on the floor
Responds the same to 'wait' at the door, in the car and on the street
Does not move forward until hearing the release signal
variations: Wait before getting out of the car
Wait before entering the dog park
Wait at the kerb before crossing the street
Wait when receiving toys or treats from your hand
Wait with food on the floor before giving the release
safetyNotes: Don't use 'wait' as a substitute for 'stay': in long-duration situations use the correct command
Practise 'wait' at the door from day one at home to prevent lifetime escape habits
Never make your dog wait if they are in a state of extreme stress or fear: it will make things worse
Always make sure to give the release signal before the dog moves on their own
wait.funFact: Dogs that learn to wait before eating develop greater self-control in general. It's like the marshmallow test for dogs: those that wait learn better overall.
wait.nextLevel: Combine 'wait' with 'stay' for longer durations. Introduce the hand signal (palm facing the dog) to work 'wait' from a distance.
wait.proTip: The secret of 'wait' is consistency: allow your dog to move even once without the release signal and they'll learn that 'wait' isn't always mandatory. Be absolutely consistent every single time.

settle.title: Settle
settle.subtitle: Active calm on cue in any situation
settle.objective: Teach the dog to actively relax on cue — not just lie down, but release bodily tension — in any environment. Useful in cafés, at home with visitors, or during long stays.
why: A dog that knows how to settle handles stress better in new environments
Allows you to take your dog to public spaces (patios, shops) without disruption
Reduces general reactivity by teaching the calm state as a concrete behaviour
Complements the 'down': relaxation goes beyond posture
benefits: Your dog can accompany you to restaurants, terraces and events without causing issues
Visitors feel comfortable because the dog doesn't bother them continuously
Quieter evenings at home when the dog learns to settle in the afternoons
Useful at vet appointments, grooming salons or long car journeys
where: 🏠 Start at home in the dog's favourite living room or room
☕ Progress to quiet patios or cafés
🐾 Designated zone with a specific mat or bed for the dog
materials: 🛏️ The dog's specific mat or bed (the 'safe zone')
🫖 High-value treats in small amounts
🔇 Very calm initial environment (no loud TV, no visitors)
💛 Exceptional patience: this command takes longer than the basics
beforeYouStart: The dog should already know 'down' fluently before working on settling
Choose a time of day when the dog is naturally calmer (post-walk)
Designate a specific mat or bed: always the same, don't move it initially
Sessions of no more than 10–15 minutes: relaxation cannot be forced or rushed
Turn off the TV and reduce stimuli during initial training

methods.title: Mat protocol (progressive relaxation method)
methods.description: The mat becomes the physical cue for relaxation. The dog learns that being on the mat = releasing tension and receiving calm. You reinforce genuine relaxation states (sigh, slow blink, head down) and ignore alert states.
methods.bestFor: All dogs, especially anxious, hyperactive or reactive ones at home

steps.title: Introduce the mat as a positive place
steps.description: Lead your dog to the mat and reward simply for being on it. Don't ask for anything more yet. Mat = treat shower.
steps.tip: Do this 5–10 times before asking for any specific behaviour. The mat must be the best place in the world.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog avoids the mat, reward even for approaching it. Build the positive association first before continuing.

steps.title: Ask for 'down' on the mat
steps.description: Once the dog voluntarily goes onto the mat, ask for 'down'. Reward when they're lying down on it.
steps.tip: Don't introduce the word 'settle' yet. First build the behaviour of being down on the mat.

steps.title: Observe and reinforce genuine relaxation
steps.description: Stay nearby but without talking. When the dog shows genuine relaxation signs (audible sigh, slow blinking, head dropping onto paws, body 'melting'), say 'settle' and reward very gently.
steps.tip: The reward must be given calmly: not with excitement. Excitement breaks relaxation. Gently toss the treat to the floor between their paws.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog gets up, say nothing. Wait for them to lie down again. Reinforce only the calm.

steps.title: Increase the duration of relaxation
steps.description: Over time, wait for more relaxation signals before rewarding: 5 seconds → 15 → 30 → 1 minute of continuous calm before the treat.
steps.tip: Use a phone timer so you don't reward too early. Timing precision is key.

steps.title: Add gradual distractions
steps.description: Start practising with small distractions: talk on the phone, turn on the TV at low volume, enter and leave the room. Always reward sustained calm.
steps.tip: Increase distractions in very small steps. A setback is not failure: it's information.

commonErrors.error: Rewarding the dog when they get up to go get the treat
commonErrors.cause: Offering the reward at the wrong height or approaching the dog with excitement
commonErrors.fix: Always toss the treat to the floor between their paws. Never offer it from your hand when seeking relaxation.

commonErrors.error: Trying to force relaxation with intense petting
commonErrors.cause: Confusing 'wanting to calm the dog' with 'trained active relaxation'
commonErrors.fix: Anxious dogs get more overstimulated by petting when already activated. Use calm rewards and silence.

commonErrors.error: Practising during high-arousal moments
commonErrors.cause: Wanting to resolve excitement with the command
commonErrors.fix: 'Settle' doesn't work at peak arousal. Always practise when the dog is already in a neutral or gently calm state.

commonErrors.error: Moving the mat before the behaviour is consolidated
commonErrors.cause: Wanting it to work in different places too quickly
commonErrors.fix: First consolidate at home with the mat always in the same place. Then progressively move the mat to other rooms and finally outdoors.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog lies down but doesn't relax: still scanning the room
troubleshooting.solution: They're physically in position but not in genuine relaxation. Keep waiting and reinforce when you see the first slow blink or sigh. Patience here is measured in minutes, not seconds.

troubleshooting.problem: They get up every time I approach to reward
troubleshooting.solution: Change how you deliver the reward: instead of approaching, gently toss the treat to the floor from where you are.

troubleshooting.problem: Works at home but they can't settle at the restaurant terrace
troubleshooting.solution: You've raised the distraction level too quickly. Take the mat to quiet places first (garden, quiet terrace) before moving to busy public spaces.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog falls asleep before I can reward the relaxation
troubleshooting.solution: That's a total success! A dog that falls asleep on the mat has reached the maximum level of relaxation. Reward gently when they wake up.

progressMilestones.goal: The dog voluntarily goes onto the mat and lies down without being asked
Shows at least one genuine relaxation signal (sigh, slow blink) on the mat
Relaxes for 1–2 minutes on the mat with small distractions present
Goes to the mat and relaxes when they hear 'settle' in quiet outdoor settings

successSigns: The dog sighs audibly when lying down on the mat
Maintains the relaxed position even when you stand up or walk nearby
Goes to the mat voluntarily when experiencing mild stress (visitors, new sounds)
The relaxation lasts over 5 minutes without intervention
variations: Settle on a restaurant terrace with background noise
Settle in the vet's waiting room
Settle while having visitors at home
Settle in a moving car
Settle without the mat (using only the verbal cue)
safetyNotes: Never use 'settle' to calm a dog in a fear crisis or panic: they first need to move away from the stimulus
If your dog never seems to relax, even at home, consult a behaviourist: there may be chronic anxiety
Don't practise this command in extremely noisy spaces or with active fear triggers
If you use the mat as a time-out or punishment zone, it will lose all its positive association
settle.funFact: Dogs have a 'stress yawn' different from a sleepy yawn. A yawn during training is a sign the dog is self-regulating — it's actually a positive thing!
settle.nextLevel: Introduce a hand signal (pointing to the mat) alongside the verbal cue. Progress to having the dog settle in public spaces without the mat: using only the verbal cue.
settle.proTip: The state of relaxation cannot be demanded: it must be cultivated. Your calm is contagious to your dog. Talk less, move more slowly, and breathe more deeply during sessions.

heel.title: Heel
heel.subtitle: Walk precisely by the handler's side, attentive and controlled
heel.objective: Teach the dog to walk precisely at the handler's left side, looking up at them, without pulling, including stops and turns. More precise and demanding than loose-leash walking.
why: Allows full control in crowded or dangerous environments without relying on force
Develops attention and the bond: the dog looks at you, not at the world
Foundation for dog sports (obedience, Rally-O, agility) and calm walks
A dog that walks in heel never pulls and makes walks enjoyable
benefits: Tension-free walks on the leash even with strong distractions
Greater safety when crossing streets or in heavy traffic areas
The dog learns to focus on you as the source of information and rewards
Builds a foundation for excellent communication during any activity
where: 🏠 Start at home or in a long distraction-free hallway
🌿 Progress to the garden or an enclosed area
🛣️ Finally practise on the street with real distractions
materials: 🫖 Very high-value treats (cooked chicken, sausage, cheese)
🦮 Short 1–1.5 m leash for the start
🎯 Clicker or consistent verbal marker ('yes' or 'good')
💛 Patience and plenty of breaks
beforeYouStart: The dog should know 'sit' fluently before starting heel
Decide from the start that heel will always be on your LEFT side: be consistent
Short sessions of 5–10 minutes with many breaks: heel is cognitively demanding
Have top-value treats in your left hand: the dog learns to follow that hand
Don't practise after a long exercise walk: the dog must be alert

methods.title: Left-hand lure method (recommended starting point)
methods.description: You hold the treat in your left hand at hip level. The dog learns that staying at your left side produces continuous rewards. Builds the heel position before adding movement.
methods.bestFor: Dogs with no heel experience or puppies starting from scratch

steps.title: Starting position: dog sitting at your left
steps.description: The dog sits at your left side, facing the same direction as you. This is the initial heel position.
steps.tip: Reward several times simply for being in that position. The space beside your left hip = reward zone.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog positions in front of you, use a wall to your right to limit their space.

steps.title: Treat at left hip level
steps.description: Hold the treat in your left hand at your hip. The dog will stretch their neck upward looking for the treat.
steps.tip: Your left hand is the dog's 'anchor'. It should always be in the same place.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog jumps for the treat, lower your hand very slightly. Only reward when all four paws are on the floor.

steps.title: First step together
steps.description: Take one step forward with your left foot and say 'heel'. If the dog follows in position, reward immediately.
steps.tip: One step, one reward. Don't ask for more distance than the dog can maintain in position.
steps.troubleshooting: If they forge ahead, stop completely and wait for them to return to your side before continuing.

steps.title: Progressively increase steps
steps.description: From 1 step → 3 → 5 → 10 → around the block. Reward at least every 3–5 steps in correct position.
steps.tip: Reward frequency is key at first: reward often to keep the dog engaged at your side.

steps.title: Introduce stops and turns
steps.description: Add a stop: when you halt, the dog should automatically sit at your side. Introduce turns: gentle curves to the left and right.
steps.tip: Anticipate turns with a slight slow-down to give the dog time to adjust.

methods.title: Circle method (to maintain pace and attention)
methods.description: You walk in tight circles toward the dog's side (left), which forces them to speed up to maintain position. Excellent for building attention and pace.
methods.bestFor: Dogs that lag behind or tend to lose position in a straight line

steps.title: Small circles to the left
steps.description: Start walking in small circles turning left. The dog has to speed up to stay at your side.
steps.tip: Left circles are more demanding for the dog (they cover more ground). Right circles are easier.
steps.troubleshooting: If the dog forges ahead, reduce the circle radius so they have less space to get in front.

steps.title: Reward correct position in the circle
steps.description: Whenever the dog is in the correct position (shoulder beside your left hip), reward.
steps.tip: The reward comes from your left hand downward. Don't make the dog jump to get it.

steps.title: Alternate circles and straight lines
steps.description: After the circles, walk in a straight line for a few steps. The dog will have already learned the pace and position from the circles.
steps.tip: The transition from circles to straight is the moment to consolidate the behaviour.

steps.title: Gradually reduce reinforcement
steps.description: Over time, reward every 10, 20 then 50 steps instead of every few steps. Keep the dog in positive uncertainty about when the reward arrives.
steps.tip: Reward variably: sometimes 5 steps, sometimes 20. Variability maintains attention better than routine.

commonErrors.error: Yanking the leash to keep the dog in position
commonErrors.cause: Wanting quick results without position work
commonErrors.fix: Heel is taught with treats and positioning, never with leash pressure. The leash must be a safety accessory, not a control tool.

commonErrors.error: Sessions too long that bore or exhaust the dog
commonErrors.cause: Wanting to advance quickly
commonErrors.fix: Heel is mentally intense. Sessions of 5–10 minutes with plenty of free-play breaks.

commonErrors.error: Moving to the street before consolidating indoors
commonErrors.cause: Jumping too quickly to the real environment
commonErrors.fix: First consolidate indoors, then garden, then quiet street, then street with distractions. Each context needs additional reinforcement.

commonErrors.error: Alternating between left and right side depending on the day
commonErrors.cause: Lack of consistency in position
commonErrors.fix: Choose ONE side (conventionally left) and be consistent. The dog learns a specific position, not 'either side'.

troubleshooting.problem: My dog looks at me but lags behind
troubleshooting.solution: The pace is too slow for them. Increase it slightly. Dogs that lag frequently improve when you speed up.

troubleshooting.problem: Holds position for 10 steps but then gets distracted and forges ahead
troubleshooting.solution: Reinforcement was spaced out too soon. Go back to rewarding every 3–5 steps until the position is more solid.

troubleshooting.problem: Works in a straight line but loses position on turns
troubleshooting.solution: Turns are harder. Practise only turns for an entire session, rewarding every correct turn independently.

troubleshooting.problem: Only works with the treat visibly in my hand; without treat they won't do it
troubleshooting.solution: Phase out the treat hand: first in hand, then in pocket but producing it when rewarding, then in a bait bag. The dog must learn the reward can appear at any moment.

progressMilestones.goal: The dog follows the left hand in correct position for 5–10 steps
Maintains position in a straight line for 20–30 steps with frequent reinforcement
Executes heel including stops (with automatic sit) and gentle turns
Walks in heel outdoors with moderate distractions for 1–2 minutes without visible treat

successSigns: The dog makes regular eye contact while walking at your side
The dog's shoulder stays aligned with your left hip for at least 30 consecutive steps
Sits automatically when you stop
Maintains position through turns without physical guidance
variations: Heel with pace changes (very slow → trot)
Heel through obstacles (cones, chairs)
Heel with other dogs or people passing nearby
Off-leash heel in a safe area (advanced)
Heel with a figure-eight between the handler's legs
safetyNotes: Never use choke, prong or electric collars to teach heel: they are counterproductive and harmful
If the dog has hip or joint problems, consult the vet before long heel sessions
Always carry water for sessions over 10 minutes on warm days
Don't practise heel with very sparse reinforcement in heavy traffic areas until the behaviour is very solid
heel.funFact: Heelwork to Music is a dog sport in which the dog performs precise choreography in time with music. Some dogs learn up to 20 different heel positions!
heel.nextLevel: Introduce off-leash heel in enclosed spaces. Then practise heel with other dogs or people passing by. Finally, combine it with other commands (heel → stay → heel).
heel.proTip: The dog's gaze into your eyes is the key to advanced heel. Reward specifically the moments of eye contact: 'looks at you = follows you = reward'. Build eye contact before you demand perfect position.
