aggression.title: Aggression
aggression.subtitle: Growling, biting or disproportionate reactions
aggression.intro: Canine aggression is one of the most serious and feared behaviors, but it's rarely 'gratuitous'. In most cases it's a communication response: the dog is warning that something bothers, hurts or scares them. Understanding the origin is the first step to redirect it.
aggression.whyHappens: The most common causes are: undiagnosed pain or illness, fear (defensive aggression), resource guarding (food, toys, rest), poor early socialization, traumatic experiences, or accumulated frustration from lack of exercise and mental stimulation. Genetics also plays a role, but environment matters much more.
aggression.whatToDo: 1. Visit the vet to rule out pain (the #1 overlooked cause). 2. Identify specific triggers (people? dogs? certain contexts?). 3. Work with gradual desensitization: controlled low-intensity exposure + positive reinforcement. 4. Build confidence with daily basic obedience. 5. Ensure rest (minimum 14h/day for adults).
aggression.whatNotToDo: 1. NEVER punish with pain, yelling or prong collars: you worsen the root cause. 2. Don't force interactions (don't make them 'make peace' with whoever they growl at). 3. Don't ignore early signs (growl = warning, not problem). If you silence the warning, the next step is the bite. 4. Don't use the muzzle as punishment, only as a safety tool.
aggression.exercises: • 'Look at that' game: name the trigger at safe distance → reward when they look at you. Repeat 5-10 min/day. • Snuffle mat work: reduces background anxiety. • Leslie McDevitt's 'Look at That': dog looks at the stimulus and voluntarily comes back to you. • Reinforce calmness: reward when lying calmly, without asking for anything.
aggression.whenToSeekHelp: SEEK IMMEDIATE HELP if: they have bitten someone leaving a mark, episodes are increasingly frequent, they attack family members, or you can't identify the trigger. You need a certified dog trainer in behavior modification or a veterinary behaviorist. This is not a case to train alone.

anxiety.title: Anxiety
anxiety.subtitle: Stress, excessive panting, can't relax
anxiety.intro: An anxious dog lives in constant alertness. They're not 'nervous by nature': their nervous system is hyper-activated and needs help returning to a calm baseline. Chronic anxiety damages physical health as much as mental.
anxiety.whyHappens: Frequent causes: separation from the guardian (most common), excessive stimulation without rest, chaotic routine, insufficient or poorly focused exercise (purely physical walks without sniffing), recent changes (move, new baby, another animal), or previous abandonment experiences. Some cases have a genetic basis requiring veterinary support.
anxiety.whatToDo: 1. Establish a very predictable routine (fixed feeding, walking, rest times). 2. Replace part of the walk with sniffing work (releases more cortisol than running). 3. Create a safe haven at home (corner with blanket, no traffic). 4. Practice 'departure desensitization': leave and return without greeting, in short sessions. 5. Natural supplementation (consult vet): valerian, melatonin, tryptophan-rich diet.
anxiety.whatNotToDo: 1. Don't pet or talk to the dog when panting or whining: you reinforce the state. 2. Don't take extra-long walks thinking 'you'll tire them out': you increase cortisol. 3. Don't make dramatic goodbyes when leaving the house. 4. Don't use the crate as punishment. 5. Don't medicate without veterinary consultation.
anxiety.exercises: • Mat-work: teach them to relax on a specific mat as a 'place of calm'. • T-Touch massage or long, gentle strokes against the grain (1 min, observe reaction). • Free sniffing 20 min/day in park (without long leash if there's risk). • Classical music or 528Hz frequency during the hours they're alone. • Frozen filled Kong: entertains them 30+ min.
anxiety.whenToSeekHelp: If your dog destroys the house when left alone, self-harms, doesn't eat for days, vomits from stress, or the problem worsens despite your efforts. Severe separation anxiety requires veterinary protocol (may include temporary medication) + behavioral plan with a trainer.

barking.title: Excessive barking
barking.subtitle: Barks at people, noises or for no apparent reason
barking.intro: Barking is normal and necessary communication, like talking for us. The problem appears when it's excessive, inappropriate to context or affects neighbors. The key is NOT to 'silence the dog' but to understand what they're trying to say and resolve the cause.
barking.whyHappens: Types of barking and their causes: alert (external noises), attention demand (learned: barks → you look), boredom (nothing to do), fear, frustration behind window or fence, or excessive excitement when greeting. Identifying the type is 80% of the solution.
barking.whatToDo: 1. Observe and record: when does it bark? at what? 2. Reduce visual triggers: opaque vinyl on windows if barking at street. 3. Increase mental exercise (sniffing games, kong, teach new tricks). 4. Teach 'quiet' as command: when it barks and stops, reward the silence (not the barking). 5. If barking for demand, IGNORE TOTALLY until it stops 5 seconds, then attend.
barking.whatNotToDo: 1. DO NOT use electric or citronella anti-bark collars: they mask the symptom without solving the problem and generate anxiety. 2. Don't yell 'QUIET' (for the dog it's barking with you, you encourage them). 3. Don't give toy or reward when barking to make them stop (you train them to bark). 4. Don't physically cover their mouth.
barking.exercises: • 'Quiet' protocol: provoke the bark (soft doorbell) → when it stops 1 sec, reward and say 'quiet'. Increase duration. • Fixed place when doorbell rings (mat = go and lie down instead of running to the door). • Cube game: hide treats around house so they spend energy searching instead of guarding. • Sound desensitization with low-volume audios gradually increasing.
barking.whenToSeekHelp: If the barks are due to intense fear (accompanied by trembling, hiding), cause neighbor complaints despite your interventions, or are a symptom of separation anxiety. A positive trainer can design a plan in 4-6 weeks.

pulling.title: Pulls on leash
pulling.subtitle: Turns the walk into a fight
pulling.intro: It's the #1 problem reported by guardians. The good news: it's solved in weeks with correct technique and consistency. The bad: it requires patience and there are NO magic shortcuts (no harness or collar teaches not to pull on its own).
pulling.whyHappens: The dog pulls because: 1) it worked once (advanced by pulling), 2) they're overstimulated and want to arrive sooner, 3) they were never taught the opposite, 4) the equipment is uncomfortable and they compensate by pulling forward, 5) your pace is too slow for them. Tense leash feeds back: dog pulls because feels tension, and you pull because they pull.
pulling.whatToDo: 1. Correct equipment: H or Y harness (not basic chest-back) + 2-3m leash (not retractable). 2. 'Tree' technique: when they tense, you stop like a tree; when they loosen, you advance. Repeat until they understand. 3. Unpredictable direction changes: every time they pull, you turn around. 4. Reward with voice/food every time the leash is loose. 5. Before going out, 5 min of play at home to spend excitement.
pulling.whatNotToDo: 1. DO NOT use choke, prong or electric collars: they damage trachea and teach by fear. 2. Don't yank back abruptly when pulling (generates opposite reaction). 3. Don't yell their name constantly (they associate it with scolding). 4. Don't use retractable leash to teach (it rewards pulling). 5. Don't give up after 2 walks: learning requires 3-4 weeks minimum.
pulling.exercises: • Walking in tight circle: 5 turns clockwise, 5 counter-clockwise. Improves attention to handler. • Heel game (by your side): take steps and reward each time the dog stays at your level. Increase duration. • 'Hook to me': walk in zigzag so they have to pay attention to your direction. • Short but perfect walks: better 15 min without pulling than 1h pulling.
pulling.whenToSeekHelp: If the dog weighs more than you and you've had falls, if they pull toward other dogs with reactivity, or if after 6 weeks of consistent work you see no improvement. An in-person session with a positive trainer can unblock invisible technical errors.

fearful.title: Fearful dog
fearful.subtitle: Hides, trembles or avoids situations
fearful.intro: A fearful dog is not 'dumb' or 'cowardly': they live with a nervous system that perceives threats where others don't see them. Forcing them to 'face' the fear (flooding) usually worsens the problem. The way out is building confidence very gradually.
fearful.whyHappens: Causes: poor socialization between weeks 3 and 14 of life (irreversible critical period), specific traumas (run over, attack by another dog), genetics, undiagnosed chronic pain, or tense family environment. Breeds like greyhounds, podencos or shepherds may be more sensitive by nature.
fearful.whatToDo: 1. Identify the tolerance threshold: at what distance does the stimulus stop affecting them? Always work below it. 2. Associate the stimulus with something positive: see the trigger at distance → treats rain. 3. Create safe and predictable routines. 4. Allow them to have refuges where no one bothers them. 5. Reinforce any voluntary exploration with happy voice.
fearful.whatNotToDo: 1. DO NOT force them to approach the feared stimulus ('so they see nothing happens'): you increase the trauma. 2. Don't scold when trembling or hiding (you reinforce that it's dangerous). 3. Don't allow strangers to touch without consent (let the dog choose to approach). 4. Don't use tense leashes: you transmit your stress. 5. Don't 'comfort' with shouts ('don't tremble, come here').
fearful.exercises: • Surface work: stepping on different textures (rug, wood, crinkly plastic) with treats. Builds physical confidence. • 'Empowerment by choice': two options, let them decide (this path or this?). • Obedience training with very high-value treats (cheese, sausage): small successes that add safety. • Attend group education classes ONLY if the trainer accepts fearful dogs without pressure.
fearful.whenToSeekHelp: If the fear prevents them from living (can't go out, doesn't eat in front of people, avoids interaction with you), if they've become aggressive from fear, or if it appeared suddenly without apparent cause (rule out pain with vet). It's a long process (months) deserving professional guidance.

destructive.title: Destructive behavior
destructive.subtitle: Chews furniture, clothes or tears papers
destructive.intro: Breaking things is symptom, not cause. Almost always indicates boredom, separation anxiety, excess energy not channeled, or natural need to chew (especially in puppies and adolescents). Punishing the dog for past destruction is ineffective: they don't associate.
destructive.whyHappens: Most common causes: 1) puppy in teething phase (3-7 months): needs to chew to relieve discomfort. 2) Chronic boredom: many hours alone without stimulation. 3) Separation anxiety: only destroys when you leave. 4) Insufficient exercise or without mental component. 5) Lack of valid objects to chew.
destructive.whatToDo: 1. Provide appropriate chews: Kong, deer antler, ropes (minimum 3 types rotating). 2. Increase mental exercise: frozen filled Kong lasts 30+ min. 3. 'Prevention before correction': remove valuables until they learn. 4. Tire the mind, not just the body: 15 min of sniffing tires more than 1h running. 5. If they only destroy when you leave, work specific separation anxiety.
destructive.whatNotToDo: 1. DO NOT scold upon return finding destruction: dog does NOT connect your anger with something done hours ago. They only learn your arrival is scary. 2. Don't give an old shoe to chew: they don't distinguish 'this shoe yes, this no'. 3. Don't use bitter sprays as sole solution (band-aid). 4. Don't leave them alone 8h without prepared activities.
destructive.exercises: • Frozen Kong: fill with paté, wet food and water, freeze. Entertains 30-60 min. • Snuffle mat: hide their kibble ration, takes 15-20 min to find. • Cardboard box with treats wrapped in paper: brutal stimulation. • Frozen vegetable bone: frozen carrot, chewable and healthy. • New toys rotating every 3-4 days to maintain novelty.
destructive.whenToSeekHelp: If the dog destroys only when left alone (probable separation anxiety), swallows dangerous objects (vital risk), self-harms (excessive licking, paw chewing), or the problem persists after 2 months of adequate environmental enrichment.

choking.title: Choking
choking.subtitle: Something is blocking the dog's airway
steps: Open the mouth carefully and look for the object. If visible and reachable, remove it with your fingers or tweezers.
If you can't see it: for small dogs, hold them upside-down by the hind legs and give 4-5 firm slaps between the shoulder blades.
For medium or large dogs: hug them from behind, hands joined just below the last rib, and compress upward 4-5 times (canine Heimlich).
Recheck the mouth after each attempt.
Go to the vet even if the object comes out — there may be internal injuries.
dontDo: Don't poke fingers blindly: you may push the object deeper
Don't give water or food to «push it down»
Don't strike a small puppy's chest with excessive force
choking.whenToCallVet: Call the vet immediately if gums turn purple, the dog loses consciousness, or you can't get the object out within 1 minute.

bleeding.title: Bleeding
bleeding.subtitle: Wounds with visible blood loss
signs: Pool of blood or soaked clothing
steps: Put on gloves if available. Keep the dog as still as possible to avoid worsening the bleeding.
Apply direct pressure with gauze, cloth or clean shirt for at least 5 minutes without lifting.
If the cloth soaks through, add another on top without removing the first. Keep pressing.
If it's a leg, raise the limb above heart level if possible.
Once controlled, bandage firmly (not too tight) and head to the vet without waiting.
dontDo: Don't remove an embedded object (glass, stick): can worsen bleeding
Don't use tourniquets except in extreme emergency (necrosis risk)
Don't apply alcohol, hydrogen peroxide or strong disinfectants on deep wounds
bleeding.whenToCallVet: Any bleeding that doesn't stop in 5 minutes, blood from mouth/anus/urine, or wounds deeper than 2 cm is an immediate veterinary emergency.

poisoning.title: Poisoning
poisoning.subtitle: Ingested something toxic (chocolate, grapes, rat poison…)
steps: Identify the toxin: keep the container, leaf, plant or vomit sample to show the vet.
Call the Veterinary Poison Helpline NOW (+1 888 426 4435) and describe what was eaten and how much.
Follow their instructions exactly. DO NOT induce vomiting without confirmation.
Keep the dog calm, warm, and in a safe place until reaching the vet.
Go to the nearest vet with the toxin's container.
dontDo: DO NOT induce vomiting if they ate something caustic (bleach, acids), petroleum products or a sharp object
Don't give milk, salt, oil, or «home remedies»: may worsen the poisoning
Don't wait for symptoms: many poisons take hours to show effects
poisoning.whenToCallVet: ALL poisoning is an immediate emergency. Even if they look fine, effects may take hours.

heat_stroke.title: Heat stroke
heat_stroke.subtitle: Hyperthermia from heat (car, exercise, sun)
steps: Move IMMEDIATELY to shade or a cool, ventilated place.
Wet them with lukewarm water (NOT cold/icy) all over, especially neck, armpits and groin.
Use a fan or wave a towel to speed up evaporation.
Offer small sips of cool water if conscious and able to swallow.
Urgent transport to the vet even if they seem to recover: internal damage may have occurred.
dontDo: NEVER use icy water or ice: causes vasoconstriction and worsens the condition
Don't wrap the dog in wet towels that trap heat
Don't force them to drink large amounts at once (aspiration risk)
heat_stroke.whenToCallVet: Call the vet on the way. Rectal temperature above 106°F (41°C) is potentially fatal and requires hospitalization.

seizures.title: Seizures
seizures.subtitle: Loss of body control, shaking, drooling
signs: Falling to the ground and muscle stiffness
Heavy drooling, loss of urine or feces
Fixed gaze, no response to your voice
steps: DO NOT try to hold them. Move furniture, stairs or objects that may injure them.
Time it from the start. A typical seizure lasts 30-90 seconds.
Talk softly even if they seem not to hear; it helps them when they recover.
Once it ends, keep them in a calm, dark, quiet place to recover.
Always go to the vet after a first seizure, even if they seem recovered.
dontDo: DO NOT put hands or objects in the mouth: dogs do NOT swallow their tongue and you may be bitten
Don't shout, shake or try to wake them abruptly
Don't give food, water or medication during or just after
seizures.whenToCallVet: IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY if: the seizure lasts more than 2 minutes, several occur without regaining consciousness between them, or it's the first time.

cpr.title: Cardiac arrest / CPR
cpr.subtitle: The dog isn't breathing and has no pulse
signs: No pulse felt on inner thigh
steps: Lay them on their right side on a firm surface. Check the airway is clear (pull tongue forward).
Give 2 rescue breaths: close the mouth, blow through the nose until you see the chest rise.
Chest compressions: for medium/large dogs press on the highest part of the rib cage with both hands. For small dogs use one hand over the heart (left elbow).
Rate: 100-120 compressions per minute (to the beat of «Stayin' Alive»). Depth: 1/3 of chest thickness.
Every 30 compressions, give 2 breaths. Continue until they breathe or you reach the vet.
dontDo: Don't stop CPR due to fatigue in less than 10 minutes without veterinary attention
Don't compress on conscious or breathing dogs (you can break ribs)
Don't place your palm on the abdomen: you can damage organs
cpr.whenToCallVet: MAXIMUM EMERGENCY. If alone, do 1 minute of CPR, then call 911 while driving to the nearest vet.

obedience_basic_30.name: Obedience in 30 days
obedience_basic_30.description: Master the essentials: sit, down, come, wait, heel…

1.title: Classic sit
1.instruction: Practice "sit" for 5 minutes with small treats. 5-8 reps.

2.title: Recognise their name
2.instruction: Say their name, wait for eye contact, treat. 10 short reps.

3.title: Sit in different spots
3.instruction: Ask "sit" in 3 different spots at home. 2-3 reps each.

4.title: Lie down
4.instruction: Teach "down" from sit. Lure with a low treat. 5 minutes.

5.title: Come when called
5.instruction: Indoors, call them from another room and treat on arrival.

6.title: Wait 5 seconds
6.instruction: Ask them to wait before crossing a doorway. Start with 2-3 sec.

7.title: Week 1 review
7.instruction: Chain sit + name + sit. Treat each success. XP bonus!

8.title: Longer down
8.instruction: Ask down and hold for 10 seconds before treating.

9.title: Name with distractions
9.instruction: Call their name with a toy nearby. Treat the eye contact.

10.title: Stay in sit
10.instruction: Ask "stay" for 10 seconds in sit. Build slowly.

11.title: Recall from further
11.instruction: Call from the other end of the room or garden. Treat every time.

12.title: Place
12.instruction: Teach them to go to their bed/mat on "place". 3-4 reps.

13.title: Wait before food
13.instruction: Ask "wait" before placing the bowl. 3-5 sec.

14.title: Week 2 review
14.instruction: Combine sit, down and stay. XP bonus!

15.title: Heel in hallway
15.instruction: Walk 5-10 steps and treat if they stay at your side.

16.title: Sit with hand signals
16.instruction: Ask sit using only the hand gesture, no voice.

17.title: Down outdoors
17.instruction: Ask down at the park or garden. Accept more distractions.

18.title: Recall with light distractions
18.instruction: Call them while sniffing (not playing). High treat if they come.

21.title: Week 3 review
21.instruction: Walk 2 minutes at heel, sit and down at the end. XP bonus!

22.title: Wait with treat in hand
22.instruction: Drop a treat on the floor and ask "wait" before they take it.

23.title: Name with multiple people
23.instruction: Another person says a fake name; you say theirs. Treat the look.

24.title: Recall during play
24.instruction: Call mid-play. HUGE treat for coming.

25.title: Stay out of sight
25.instruction: Ask stay and step away with your back turned for 5 sec.

26.title: Place with distractions
26.instruction: Ask place with TV on or soft background noise.

27.title: Heel with direction changes
27.instruction: Walk and make 3 turns. Treat when they adjust.

28.title: Perfect sit on the street
28.instruction: Ask sit in a busy area. Be generous with rewards.

29.title: Recall in park
29.instruction: Off leash if safe, call them and treat well.

30.title: Final exam!
30.instruction: Chain sit, down, stay, place and recall. You're a team!

socialization_30.name: Socialization in 30 days
socialization_30.description: Small daily exposures for a balanced pup.

1.title: Calm walk
1.instruction: 10-min walk in a quiet area. Treat calm responses to people.

2.title: People at distance
2.instruction: Sit on a bench and watch people pass. Treat the calm.

3.title: Soft sounds
3.instruction: At home, play soft music or everyday sounds. Treat ignoring them.

4.title: Children playing (far)
4.instruction: Approach a playground from afar. Treat calm.

5.title: Walk at a new time
5.instruction: Walk at an unusual time. Change = learning.

6.title: Another dog at 20 m
6.instruction: Pass another dog at distance. Treat looking at YOU.

7.title: Review: the calmest
7.instruction: Today: 15 min in a new place. Goal = 0 barks. XP bonus!

8.title: Bike or scooter
8.instruction: Watch bikes pass at distance. Treat ignoring.

9.title: Outside a shop
9.instruction: Approach a shop entrance. Practice 1-min wait.

10.title: People with hats
10.instruction: Find people with unusual things and reward.

11.title: Walk with friend
11.instruction: Walk with a friend and a calm dog. 10 min parallel.

12.title: Cars and motorcycles
12.instruction: Walk on a moderately busy street. Treat the calm.

13.title: Greet with permission
13.instruction: If someone wants to say hi, ask "sit" first.

14.title: Review: new smells
14.instruction: 20 min at a new park. Let them sniff lots. XP bonus!

15.title: Coffee on terrace
15.instruction: If possible, sit at a pet-friendly terrace 15 min.

16.title: Short dog encounter
16.instruction: 5-second greeting with a known dog and walk away. Treat.

17.title: Small kids nearby
17.instruction: 5 m from a playground. Reinforce calm.

18.title: Use the noise
18.instruction: If a siren passes, treat immediately. Noise = good.

19.title: Visit friend's house
19.instruction: Take them to a new house (a friend's). 20 min relaxed.

20.title: Another dog passes near
20.instruction: 3 m from another dog passing. Treat no reaction.

21.title: Review: urban area
21.instruction: 25-min walk in a calm urban area. XP bonus!

22.title: Friendly vet
22.instruction: Walk past the clinic. If possible, pop in for hello with no exam.

23.title: People with umbrellas
23.instruction: Rain or not, find unusual shapes and treat.

24.title: Pet-friendly cafe
24.instruction: Find a dog-friendly venue and stay 20 min.

25.title: Bikes at 5 m
25.instruction: Reduce distance to bikes. Always treat the calm.

26.title: 30-second greeting
26.instruction: Longer hello with a calm dog. If tense, separate.

27.title: Market or event
27.instruction: If a market is nearby, 15-min walk along the edge.

28.title: Group of people
28.instruction: Approach a chatting group. Treat the calm.

29.title: Two new dogs
29.instruction: Controlled greeting with 2 different dogs in the day.

30.title: Final challenge!
30.instruction: Take your pup to a new and challenging place. You've grown!

fun_tricks_30.name: Fun tricks
fun_tricks_30.description: Paw, high-five, spin, roll over… 30 days of fun.

1.title: Paw (1)
1.instruction: Hide a treat in a closed fist. When they paw it, treat.

2.title: Paw (2)
2.instruction: Repeat with the cue word "paw". 10 short reps.

3.title: High five (1)
3.instruction: Raise hand a bit. When they touch, say "five" and treat.

4.title: High five (2)
4.instruction: Same gesture, hand higher. Treat the firm touch.

5.title: High touch (1)
5.instruction: Like high-five but pawing higher, palm vertical.

7.title: Week 1 review
7.instruction: Chain paw + five + high touch. XP bonus!

8.title: Spin (1)
8.instruction: Lure in a circle with a treat. Treat the full turn.

9.title: Spin (2)
9.instruction: Reduce the lure. Use only gesture + word "spin".

10.title: Bow (1)
10.instruction: Treat when they stretch front legs (typical morning stretch).

11.title: Bow (2)
11.instruction: Pair the cue "bow" when they offer it.

12.title: Roll over (1)
12.instruction: From down, lure across their side. Treat partial rolls.

14.title: Week 2 review
14.instruction: Chain spin + bow + roll. XP bonus!

15.title: Fetch (1)
15.instruction: Throw a toy 1 m. Treat picking it up.

16.title: Fetch (2)
16.instruction: Throw a bit further. Treat returning to you.

18.title: Left vs right paw
18.instruction: Ask specific paw (left or right). Treat the right side.

19.title: High five at distance
19.instruction: Stretch your arm. Treat reaching to touch.

21.title: Week 3 review
21.instruction: Mix 5 tricks in 5 min. XP bonus!

22.title: Held bow
22.instruction: Train the bow held for 3 seconds.

23.title: Roll over no lure
23.instruction: Gesture only. Treat the full roll.

25.title: Crossed paw
25.instruction: Ask the opposite paw to the hand you offer.

26.title: Spin + sit
26.instruction: Combine turn + final sit. Treat the sequence.

29.title: Fetch with distractions
29.instruction: Throw with another dog or person near. Treat focus.

30.title: Final show
30.instruction: Chain 6 tricks in a row. You're a circus duo!

mental_active_30.name: Active mind
mental_active_30.description: Scent games and enrichment to tire the brain.

1.title: Treat in closed hand
1.instruction: Hide a treat in one hand. Treat when they paw the right hand.

2.title: 3 cups
2.instruction: Hide treat under 1 of 3 inverted cups. Let them sniff!

3.title: Search the food
3.instruction: Scatter food on grass or carpet. 5-10 minutes sniffing.

4.title: Enrichment toy
4.instruction: Stuff a Kong or toy with food. 15 minutes of work.

5.title: Toy name
5.instruction: Repeat the name of their favourite toy. Treat the touch.

6.title: Hide yourself
6.instruction: Hide in another room and call them. Treat the find.

7.title: Review: pure scent
7.instruction: 10 hidden treats around the house. XP bonus!

8.title: Cardboard box
8.instruction: Treats in a box with crumpled paper. Let them dig.

9.title: Rolled blanket
9.instruction: Hide treats in the folds of a rolled blanket.

10.title: Knotted towels
10.instruction: 2-3 towels with loose knots and treats inside.

11.title: Choose
11.instruction: Place 2 toys and say one's name. Treat the right pick.

12.title: Hide the toy
12.instruction: Hide their toy in plain sight, then trickier.

13.title: Snuffle mat or carpet
13.instruction: If you have a snuffle mat, food on it 10 min. Else towels.

14.title: Review: detective
14.instruction: Find 3 objects around the house with your help. XP bonus!

15.title: Frozen Kong
15.instruction: Fill a Kong with wet food and freeze. 20 min of work.

16.title: Cup pattern
16.instruction: 3 inverted cups. Move treat between them. Sniff right one.

17.title: Surprise box
17.instruction: Box with various safe objects. Treat at the bottom.

18.title: Backyard tracking
18.instruction: Drag a treat then hide it. Let them follow the trail.

19.title: Two toy names
19.instruction: Distinguish 2 toys by name. Start easy.

20.title: Hide and seek
20.instruction: Ask "wait". Hide treat out of sight. Find it together.

22.title: Bottle with holes
22.instruction: Plastic bottle with treats and small holes. Roll for treats.

23.title: Learn new cue
23.instruction: Invent a cue ("touch", "look"). Work it 10 min.

24.title: Complex pattern
24.instruction: Hide cups in various spots. Find one by one.

25.title: Cooperative work
25.instruction: Short cues (sit, look, paw). Treat each success.

26.title: Longer track
26.instruction: 1-min track with several turns. Treat at the end.

27.title: Find hidden person
27.instruction: Another person hides; pup finds them. Treat the find.

28.title: Towels + box
28.instruction: Combine knotted towels inside a box. Double challenge.

29.title: Pick by name
29.instruction: If they know names, ask one of 3. Treat the right pick.

30.title: Mental marathon!
30.instruction: 4 different games in 30 min. Hydrate and enjoy. XP bonus!
